# Enrichment-free, Targeted Covalent Drug Discovery in Live Cells

**Authors:** Kevin D. Dong; Qing Yu; Ka Yang; Bertrand J. Wong; Hong Yue; Sipei Fu; Rebecca L. Whitehouse; Eric S. Fischer; Steven P. Gygi

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Cell Biology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 2Program in Cellular and Molecular Medicine, Boston Children’s Hospital, Boston, MA, USA | 3Department of Cancer Biology, Dana-Farber Cancer Institute, Boston, MA, USA | 4Department of Biological Chemistry and Molecular Pharmacology, Harvard Medical School, Boston, MA, USA | 5Present address: Department of Biochemistry and Molecular Biotechnology, University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, Worcester, MA, USA | 6Present address: Department of Pathology, Stanford School of Medicine, Palo Alto, CA, USA

## Abstract

Live cell activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) with mass spectrometry enables the proteome-wide quantification of compound reactivity, yet resulting datasets often suffer from low data completeness for high-priority targets and do not give users the option to measure compound-induced protein changes within the same screening assay. To address these limitations, we developed CysDig, an enrichment-free chemoproteomics platform for targeted covalent drug discovery in live cells. Using the CysDig platform, we screened 288 cysteine-reactive electrophiles against 300 functionally annotated cysteine sites. From this screen, we identified covalent binders that liganded dozens of sites and identified multiple instances of acute compound-induced protein degradation of ACAT1. We validated a molecule that engaged with the active site of the HECT E3 ligase HUWE1 and showed that chemical inhibition stabilized known substrates. Together, these findings establish CysDig as a powerful, targeted platform for live cell covalent drug screening, expanding the current repertoire of available approaches for ligand discovery in live cells.

## Abstract

## Introduction

Covalent molecules can irreversibly or reversibly modify proteins, providing chemical tools to probe protein function and promising therapeutic modalities for human disease1. The increasing number of covalent drug approvals continues to ignite the search for additional covalent chemical starting points for previously considered “undruggable” targets2. The discovery of these ligands is realized by a diverse repertoire of available methods3, with activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) coupled to mass spectrometry providing a proteome-wide readout to quantify covalent molecule binding4.

In a standard cysteine ABPP experiment, a covalent molecule competes with an enrichable cysteine-reactive probe, and the resulting reduction in probe labeling relative to a control serves as an indirect readout of compound engagement at that cysteine site. Throughput can be significantly increased using tandem mass tag (TMT)-enabled multiplexing, which allows simultaneous analysis of up to 18 samples in a single mass spectrometry run5. We and others have leveraged this approach to profile proteome-wide cysteine reactivity of electrophilic fragments in both live cells and lysates4,6–10.

Current cysteine profiling workflows enable broad assessment of compound engagement across the human proteome, offering unprecedented coverage of the cysteinome. However, despite this depth, these workflows often suffer from high rates of missing values, particularly for cysteine sites of functional or therapeutic interest. This limitation is especially apparent in large-scale experiments, where high data completeness is critical for comparative analysis or compound hit identification in the context of drug screens. Moreover, the requirement for cysteine enrichment precludes the ability to simultaneously quantify protein abundance in the same assay—an important consideration in live cell studies where compound treatment may induce downstream proteomic changes that inform mechanism of action11.

To this end, we developed CysDig, an enrichment-free chemoproteomics platform that integrates GoDig12, a TMT-based targeted proteomics strategy, within the context of cysteine-electrophile treatment. The method relies on the observation that covalent modification of a cysteine by a compound prevents alkylation by iodoacetamide (IAA) during standard proteomic sample preparation. By directly targeting IAA-labeled cysteine-containing peptides, CysDig obviates the need for enrichment and enables stoichiometric quantification of compound occupancy at targeted cysteine sites13. Critically, omitting the enrichment step now enables protein abundance measurements, which is already a core feature of the original GoDig platform and validated across several organisms12,14.

Here, we leveraged CysDig to screen an electrophilic fragment library in live cells against 300 user-selected, functionally annotated cysteines belonging to proteins involved in various cellular processes. We report that CysDig improved overall dataset completeness and identified covalent fragments that engaged dozens of these targeted sites while clearly differentiating instances of compound-induced acute protein depletion. To demonstrate the utility of our platform in identifying functional covalent binders, we followed up with a fragment that engaged the catalytic cysteine of the HECT E3 ligase HUWE1. Covalent docking and direct detection of the covalent adduct confirmed active site engagement. Importantly, treatment with this compound led to the dose-dependent accumulation of known HUWE1 substrates, providing evidence of target inhibition. Collectively, these results establish CysDig as a modular, target-centric chemoproteomics platform for covalent drug discovery in live cells.

## Results

### Datasets from standard cysteine profiling workflows can have high missing values across experiments

Untargeted, proteome-wide cysteine profiling methods are stochastic in nature and often return datasets with a high instance of missing values across experiments. For example, in three previously conducted live cell TMT-ABPP campaigns, data completeness for cysteine-containing peptides from proteins involved in key regulatory processes such as transcription (Fig. 1a), phosphorylation (Fig. 1b), and proteostasis (Fig. 1c) ranged from 57-70%6. High levels of missing values increase false negative rates, ultimately limiting the chances of identifying chemical hits for downstream validation and development. We reasoned that targeting a few hundred user-defined cysteine-containing peptides using a targeted proteomics strategy would improve overall dataset data completeness.

### Scout fragment engagement measurements without cysteine enrichment are comparable to those from an enrichment-based workflow

To evaluate whether enrichment-free compound engagement data are comparable to those obtained from conventional enrichment-based workflows, we performed a paired experiment using both whole proteome (enrichment-free) and TMT-ABPP (enrichment-based) approaches on the same K562 cell lysates treated with increasing doses of two previously characterized scout fragments4, KB02 and KB05 (Fig. S1a). Of the shared cysteine-containing peptides quantified across the two datasets, we targeted 363 cysteine-containing peptides by using GoDig12 to monitor cysteine-containing peptides from an unfractionated aliquot that was siphoned off from the whole proteome sample prior to deep fractionation. This sample would represent the type of unfractionated, complex sample that we would generate for our CysDig platform when conducting covalent drug screens (Fig S1b). Encouragingly, cysteine engagement measurements for both scout fragments across the whole proteome, TMT-ABPP, and CysDig methods showed general agreement, despite these being fundamentally different approaches (Fig. S1c, S1d, Supplementary Table S1). These results demonstrate that the enrichment step can be bypassed by directly analyzing IAA-labeled cysteine peptides from complex, unfractionated samples. These findings validate the feasibility of conducting enrichment-free, target-centric covalent ligand screens using CysDig.

### The CysDig strategy for plate-based, enrichment-free targeted screens in live cells

The general workflow for CysDig is shown in Figure 2. We conducted a CysDig-enabled screen in K562 cells. Cells were treated with cysteine-targeting electrophiles for 3 hr and then prepared for CysDig analysis (Fig.2a). Our library consisted of 288 compounds in total: 128 chloroacetamide-based and 160 acrylamide-based warhead-containing compounds (Supplementary Table S2). The average molecular weight of the library was 231.2 Da (Fig. S2). In comparison to enrichment-based TMT-ABPP, there is no need to use enrichment reagents such as DBIA, which streamlines sample preparation to only two days. For this screen, we selected 300 peptides containing functionally annotated cysteines across proteins involved in key cellular processes such as metabolism, intracellular signaling, protein quality control, and genome regulation. We reasoned that compound binding at many of these given cysteines would likely cause a functional and measurable change in protein activity. Thus, hits from this screen, upon validation, could be used as chemical starting points for downstream probe development. Of note, a subset of sites was included to specifically help us gauge the promiscuity of a given compound. For example, Cys24 of CLIC1, Cys413 of ACAT1, and Cys283 of CKB were chosen as these sites have been found to be liganded by multiple compounds6. Including such sites in targeted covalent drug screens would enable the prioritization of less promiscuous compounds for downstream development.

### A targeted data acquisition strategy improves data completeness

A limitation of current untargeted cysteine profiling workflows is the high rate of missing values across experiments. To evaluate whether our targeted data acquisition strategy could address this issue, we compared the mean data completeness of shared cysteine-containing peptides from our CysDig screen to that of three previously published live-cell TMT-ABPP screening campaigns6. CysDig improved peptide-level data completeness, achieving a mean of 94.1% compared to 70–80% with standard enrichment-based cysteine profiling workflows (Fig. 3a, 3b). This result was expected since targeted approaches generally improve data completeness, thereby reducing false negatives and increasing the likelihood of identifying covalent binders against targets of interest.

### Identification of electrophilic fragments that ligand cysteines with functional annotations on human proteins

Of the targeted cysteine-containing peptides, 54 showed a log2CR of at least 1 by at least one compound (Fig. 4a, Supplementary Table S2). Most of these compounds contained a chloroacetamide-based warhead, which is generally more reactive toward cysteine thiolates than acrylamide-based warheads (Fig. 4b). Among these cysteine sites, 17 were strongly engaged, demonstrating a log2CR of at least 2 by at least one compound. Creatine kinase B (CKB), specifically Cys283, emerged as the most frequently liganded site, suggesting high intrinsic reactivity of this cysteine which plays a critical role in cellular energy homeostasis by catalyzing the reversible transfer of a phosphate group from phosphocreatine to ADP to regenerate ATP15,16. Other notable liganded sites included: Cys271 of NSUN2, which is required for RNA m5C modification17–19; Cys288, the electrophile-sensing cysteine of KEAP1, which regulates the stability of NRF220,21; Cys843, the active site of UBE3A, a HECT E3 ligase hijacked by HPV E6 to degrade TP53 in HPV-driven cancers22; and Cys43 of FABP523, which enables the intracellular trafficking of fatty acids (Fig. 4c). SAR trends can be extrapolated from strongly liganded cysteines with multiple hits. Previously published SAR around PIN1 ligands is recapitulated in this screen where three cyclic sulfones were identified as hits (CL41, CL71, CL74)6. Other examples of structural subsets include compounds with thiazole and benzo-fused oxygen heterocycles showing a preference for Cys24 of CLIC1, and compounds with halogenated benzene subgroups showing a preference for Cys283 of CKB. Chemical hits against these functionally annotated cysteine sites could represent promising starting points for probe development upon further validation. Here, we show that CysDig enables the discovery of covalent small molecules that engage functionally relevant cysteines in live human cells.

### Characterization of a HUWE1 active site inhibitor

Among the liganded cysteines identified in our screen were several cysteines known to play regulatory or catalytic roles in protein function. Given the central role of the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) in maintaining protein homeostasis24 and its growing prominence as a therapeutic target25, we focused on liganded cysteine sites within this pathway. Specifically, E3 ligases are attractive targets because modulating their activity can directly influence the stability of their protein substrates such as tumor suppressors or oncogenes. Moreover, E3 ligases are increasingly being co-opted as modular components for targeted protein degradation applications, making covalent binders to these enzymes valuable both as functional probes and as starting points for the design of heterobifunctional degraders26.

The human genome encodes 28 HECT E3 ligases, many of which regulate critical cellular processes yet remain relatively underexplored from a chemical biology perspective. HECT E3 ligases directly form a covalent thioester intermediate with ubiquitin via a conserved catalytic cysteine, rendering them mechanistically well-suited for covalent inhibition27. While a handful of inhibitors have been reported for this class of proteins28–32, no covalent active site binders have been characterized. We prioritized the HECT E3 ligase HUWE1 as this ligase regulates protein complex quality control, the DNA damage response, cell proliferation, and apoptosis33. Notably, its dysregulation has been implicated in both neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer34.

From our screen, we identified 33 chloroacetamide-containing electrophiles that bound the HUWE1 active site with at least 50% occupancy. Among these, three exhibited strong engagement, occupying greater than 75% of the active site (Fig. 5a). To prioritize selective ligands for follow-up studies, we evaluated compound occupancy at two additional targeted active-site cysteines from related HECT E3 ligases, UBE3A and UBE3C. Compound CL129 emerged as the most selective, showing strong engagement at HUWE1 with minimal off-target binding to UBE3A or UBE3C (Fig. 5b, c). Additionally, untargeted, proteome-wide cysteine profiling experiments in both HEK293T and K562 lysates treated with escalating doses of CL129 demonstrate relatively few liganded sites (greater than 75% occupancy) (Fig. S3, Supplementary Table S3). Moreover, we highlight dose-dependent engagement to the HUWE1 active site with relative selectivity over other quantified HECT E3 ligases (Fig. S4). We then referred to a published crystal structure of the HUWE1 HECT domain35 for docking studies. Covalent docking of CL129 to HUWE1’s catalytic Cys4341 predicted key non-covalent interactions, including hydrogen bonding with Gly4316 and Glu4315, interaction with Arg4088, and an anion–π stacking between the pyrimidine ring and Glu4315 (Fig. 5d). Mass spectrometry analysis of the purified HUWE1 HECT domain confirmed direct covalent modification at the catalytic cysteine by CL129 (Fig. 5e). To evaluate the functional consequences of HUWE1 active site inhibition, we conducted a six hr dose-dependent proteomic analysis of K562 cells treated with CL129. Levels of previously reported HUWE1 substrates—C16orf72/HAPSTR136,37, DDIT438,39, MCL140, and SCNM136—increased in a dose-dependent manner without affecting HUWE1 protein levels (Fig. 5f, Fig. S5, Supplementary Table S4). Western blot analysis of DDIT4 further confirmed our proteomic results (Fig. 5g). Together, these findings validate CL129 as a covalent binder of the HUWE1 active site.

### Hybrid CysDig assays enable differentiation of cysteine engagement from acute protein depletion events

In live-cell experiments, compound-induced changes in protein abundance can be misinterpreted as target engagement, since dropout of cysteine-containing peptides occurs in both scenarios. CysDig overcomes this limitation by simultaneously quantifying non-cysteine–containing peptides for protein abundance measurements from the same sample. These hybrid CysDig assays enable confident discrimination between compound binding and compound-induced reductions in protein levels.

To illustrate the utility of a hybrid CysDig assay, we performed a second analysis of the same 36 TMT plexes that were analyzed previously. We retargeted a subset of functionally annotated cysteine-containing peptides from our previous screen, along with corresponding non-cysteine-containing peptides for robust protein abundance measurements (Fig. 6a). This strategy enabled us to assess both compound occupancy at a specific cysteine site and the overall abundance of that respective protein. As expected, for nearly all measured proteins, abundance remained unchanged, confirming that most liganding events reflected true occupancy rather than a change in protein levels (Fig.6b, Supplementary Table S2). This result is unsurprising, as the screen was conducted at a 3 hr timepoint, minimizing the likelihood of changes in protein abundance. From this hybrid CysDig assay, we could confidently assign compound binding without associated degradation to all molecules that liganded Cys283 of CKB (Fig.6c). Among the few proteins with at least one compound causing greater than a 2-fold reduction in protein abundance (ACAT1, TST, PHF5A, and HADHB), ACAT1 stood out, showing acute degradation upon treatment with 13 chloroacetamide-containing fragments (Fig. 6d, S6a–c). Our findings corroborate previous reports of ACAT1 degradation following treatment with chloroacetamide-containing PROTACs41. We confirmed this observation by treating cells with increasing doses of CL77, which induced degradation of ACAT1 that was rescued with bortezomib (BTZ), a proteasome inhibitor (Fig. 6e). Similarly, treatment with iodoacetamide (IAA) similarly caused acute degradation of ACAT1, again rescued with proteasome inhibition (Fig. 6f). These results suggest that ACAT1 may act as a sensor for strong electrophiles, with its proteasome-dependent degradation potentially serving as a readout for electrophile-induced cellular stress. Here, we show that hybrid CysDig assays can discriminate between cysteine engagement and protein depletion events. Gaining such information-rich readouts at the screening level supports efficient prioritization of chemical hits with the desired profile and minimal off-target effects.

## Discussion

CysDig is an enrichment-free, targeted chemoproteomics platform in live cells. By applying a TMT-based targeted data acquisition strategy (GoDig) within the context of cysteine-electrophile treatment, CysDig overcomes key limitations of traditional cysteine profiling workflows—most notably, high missing values and the inability to quantify compound-induced protein changes in the same assay. We note that current enrichment-based cysteine profiling methods may allow the inference of degradation events based on the liganding of multiple cysteine sites on a protein. However, if only two cysteines are quantified, it remains possible that both sites were liganded, making abundance changes indistinguishable from site occupancy effects. By contrast, the CysDig platform’s ability to quantify non-cysteine peptides provides definitive evidence of protein abundance changes. Furthermore, bypassing enrichment now simplifies sample preparation to two days, improves data completeness, and allows users to build custom targeted proteomics assays for covalent drug screens.

Using CysDig, we screened an electrophilic fragment library across 300 functionally annotated cysteine sites in live cells. We demonstrate how our targeted data acquisition strategy returns higher peptide-level data completeness compared to traditional TMT-ABPP workflows. Importantly, we identify dozens of covalent binders as starting points for chemical probe development upon further validation. We focused on HECT E3 ligases where cysteines play essential catalytic roles in ubiquitin transfer27,42. Among three targeted HECT E3 ligases—HUWE1, UBE3A, and UBE3C—we identified CL129 as a relatively selective covalent binder of the HUWE1 active site located in the HECT domain that also upregulated the abundance of known substrates in a dose-dependent manner. Despite high sequence conservation across HECT domains, our findings suggests that there may be a unique opportunity to exploit subtle structural differences for selective covalent engagement of HECT E3 ligases. Ultimately, these studies validate the discovery capabilities of the CysDig platform, and moreover, nominate CL129 for further development as a new covalent probe to further our understanding of HUWE1 biology and explore the therapeutic potential of HUWE1 inhibition in various human disease models.

Standard live-cell ABPP workflows are constrained to short treatment times (< 3 hr) to minimize confounding protein changes. With hybrid CysDig assays, screens could be extended to much later timepoints while measuring both protein expression and cysteine engagement, opening new opportunities to conduct biology-driven discovery campaigns in which the functional consequences of binding can be measured such as substrate stabilization or pathway activation. Because protein abundance is quantified in the same assay, CysDig allows confident differentiation between true cysteine engagement and compound-induced protein abundance changes. For example, ACAT1 was acutely degraded by more than 2-fold by thirteen distinct chloroacetamides, suggesting its acute proteasome-dependent degradation may serve as a proxy for electrophilic stress and should be included in covalent drug discovery campaigns to flag electrophiles that may induce unwanted cellular stress. Notably, ACAT1 is not a short-lived protein43, indicating that its rapid proteasome-mediated degradation by chloroacetamide-containing electrophiles and the general alkylating agent iodoacetamide (IAA) is likely a concerted mechanism that warrants further investigation.

CysDig adds to the repertoire of currently available platforms for small molecule covalent drug discovery. Its ability to simultaneously measure cysteine occupancy and protein abundance within one unified assay now empowers a new class of information-rich, biology-driven covalent drug screens at extended timepoints. Looking forward, the CysDig platform is broadly extensible. With chemical libraries containing the appropriate electrophilic warheads, this platform could be adapted to identify covalent labeling of other nucleophilic residues—such as serine, tyrosine, lysine, or histidine—further expanding the scope of covalent drug discovery beyond targeting cysteine44. Integration with next-generation TMTpro-35plex reagents should also enhance throughput, enabling hundreds of user-defined targets to be profiled in a single assay with fast and effective acquisition times of under 3.5 min per sample45,46. Recent improvements to the GoDig software46 and the integration of library-free methods47 are expected to further boost data completeness and the number of peptides that can be targeted with the CysDig platform, respectively.

## Methods

### Cell culture

K562 cells were grown in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% FBS, 50 U/ml penicillin and 50 U/ml streptomycin and incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator. Confluent dishes of cells were either harvested and stored at -80 °C until required for lysis or they were plated into 96-well plates for downstream proteomics-based experiments.

### Sample preparation for proteomic analyses

#### Paired in-lysate cysteine profiling and whole proteome comparison experiment

Frozen cell pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer (PBS, pH 7.4, 0.1% NP-40). A syringe equipped with a 21-gauge needle was used to produce the lysate. Further homogenization was achieved by sonication with an EpiShear™ Probe Sonicator (Active Motif) for a total of 5 min (3 seconds on, 5 seconds off, at 50% amplitude) on ice. The crude lysate was centrifuged at 1400g for 5 min at 4°C, after which the supernatant was collected into a separate tube. The protein concentration was quantified using a BCA assay kit, and the lysate was subsequently diluted to a concentration of 2 μg/μL with lysis buffer.

In each well of a 96-well plate, 25 μL of K562 lysate, with a total protein content of 50 µg, was deposited. To this, 5 μL of a compound solution in lysis buffer was added to achieve a final concentration ranging from 50 to 500 μM, followed by an incubation period of 1 hr. The probe-treated lysate was subsequently divided into two equal portions.

For DBIA-based reactive cysteine profiling, 5 μL of a DBIA solution in lysis buffer was introduced to reach a 500 μM concentration and incubated in darkness for 1 hr. For IAA-based cysteine profiling, 5 μL of lysis buffer was added and incubated for 1 hr. Following this, 3 μL of SP3 beads (a 1:1 mixture of hydrophobic and hydrophilic beads at 50 mg/mL) were incorporated, along with 30 μL of ~98% ethanol supplemented with 20 mM DTT. The lysate-bead mixture was subjected to a 10-minute incubation with gentle agitation before placing the plate on a magnetic stand to remove the supernatant. A single wash with 80% ethanol was performed, and the beads were re-suspended in 30 μL of lysis buffer supplemented with 20 mM IAA. This preparation was then shaken vigorously in the dark for 30 min. Subsequently, 60 μL of ~98% ethanol supplemented with 20 mM DTT was added to the mixture and the samples were agitated gently before being washed twice with 80% ethanol. The aqueous phase was discarded, and 30 μL of 200 mM EPPS buffer (pH 8.5) containing 0.25 μg of Lys-C was added. The samples were left to incubate at room temperature for 3 hr. Finally, 5 μL of EPPS buffer with 0.25 μg of trypsin was incorporated, and the mixture was incubated with the beads at 37 °C overnight.

#### Enamine electrophile fragment screen and CL129-treated whole proteome analysis

Cells were processed in a plate-based format as previously described11. Briefly, compounds were pre-dispensed into 96-well plates followed by the addition of 100,000 K562 cells (~10 μg) per well for 3 hr. Cells were spun down and washed twice with ice cold PBS. Cells were then lysed in lysis buffer (8M urea, 0.1% SDS, 2mM DTT, 200mM EPPS) for 30 min followed by the addition of 10mM iodoacetamide (IAA) in the dark for an additional 30 min. Lysates were quenched with 20mM DTT and subjected to SP3 bead-based precipitation. Samples were then TMT-labeled on bead and quenched with hydroxylamine followed by desalting via Sep-Pak prior to mass spectrometry analysis. Samples from the electrophile screen were not fractionated and whole proteome samples were subjected to basic pH reversed-phase fractionation prior to mass spectrometry analysis48.

#### On-bead TMT-labeling of digested peptides

Digested peptides were labeled using TMTpro18-plex reagents as previously described5. Briefly, peptides were labeled in a 1:2 ratio by mass (peptides/TMT reagents) for 1 hr with shaking at 1,200 rpm. Excess TMT reagent was quenched with hydroxylamine (0.3% final concentration) for 15 min at room temperature. Next, samples were mixed 1:1 across all TMT channels and the pooled sample was dried using a Speedvac to ensure that all acetonitrile was removed. The desalting of the resulting sample was performed using a 100 mg Sep-Pak column.

#### Basic pH reversed-phase fractionation for whole proteome experiments

For whole proteome analyses, TMT-labeled peptides, approximately 100 μg, were fractionated using an Agilent 300 Extend C18 column (3.5 μm particles, 2.1mm ID, and 250mm in length). A 50-minute linear gradient from 13 to 43% buffer B (90% acetonitrile, 10mM ammonium bicarbonate, pH 8) was employed to separate the peptides at a flow rate of 0.25ml/min. The fractions were collected into a 96-well plate and subsequently consolidated into 24 super fractions. Before LC-MS/MS analysis, the fractionated samples were desalted using StageTips.

### Mass spectrometry-based data acquisition

#### LC-MS acquisition with real-time searching of the paired in-lysate cysteine profiling and whole proteome experiments

Desalted samples were resuspended in LC-MS loading buffer (5% ACN and 5% FA) and loaded on a 100-μm capillary column packed with 30 cm of Accucore 150 resin (2.6 μm, 150Å; Thermo Fisher Scientific). Enriched cysteine samples were separated using a 180-min method on a Proxeon NanoLC-1200 UPLC system. Data were collected using an RTS-MS3 method with a 3-hr (DBIA-based cysteine profiling) or 2-hr (IAA-based whole proteome) gradient on an Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer coupled with a FAIMS Pro Duo interface. Data were collected alternating between a set of three FAIMS compensation voltages (CVs). For the whole proteome sample using IAA-only, only one set of CV values (-40, -60 and -80V) was used. For the enriched cysteine sample, two sets of CV values (-60, -45 and -35V; -70, -55 and -30) were used. MS1 scans were collected in the Orbitrap with a resolution setting of 60 K, a mass range of 400-1600 m/z, a standard AGC, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. RTS-MS3 scans were acquired with a cycle time of 1 s. MS2 spectra were acquired by selecting the top ten most abundant features via collision-induced dissociation in the ion trap using a standard AGC, quadrupole isolation width of 0.5 m/z and a maximum ion accumulation time of 50 ms. Dynamic exclusion was enabled with an exclusion duration of 120 s and amass tolerance of ±7 p.p.m. Resulting MS2 scans were searched in real time using the Comet search engine (https://uwpr.github.io/Comet/) and the returned peptides were filtered using simple initial filters that included: not matching a reversed-sequence, maximum PPM error <10, minimum cross correlation of 0.5, minimum delta Corr of 0.10 and minimum peptide length of 7. If peptide spectra matched those criteria above, an SPS–MS3 scan was inserted using up to 10 b- and y-type fragment ions as precursors with a 500% AGC of 200 K for a maximum of 200ms, with a normalized collision energy setting of 45.

#### LC-MS acquisition with real-time targeted chemoproteomics assays using GoDig

GoDig was run on the data collection computer connected to the instrument as previously described12. Experiments used a 105-min gradient (120-min method). Note that the instrument method only included Orbitrap MS1 scans (resolution of 120K; mass range 400–1500 m/z; AGC target 2e5; max injection time of 50 ms; a single FAIMS CV of -60 V). All other scan types with CV values at -40, -60 and -80, including prescans, ion trap MS2, Orbitrap MS2, and Orbitrap MS3 scans were prompted for insertion via the API using the GoDig software. Peptide targets, elution and spectral libraries were loaded into GoDig.

GoDig monitors each collected MS1 spectrum in real time with the possibility of inserting 5 different scan types for different uses12:

- GoDig injects CV-specific prescans for each FAIMS CV value needed in addition to the one being collected by the instrument method. These are used to set the AGC.

- Every 15 s, GoDig selects and fragments the top 6 precursors in the most immediate MS1 scan to collect fast ion trap MS2 scans. The resulting scans are searched and mapped to the elution library. Their elution bins are retrieved and used to calibrate the current elution point.

- In parallel, GoDig sends ion trap PRM scans for targets within the calibrated elution window (±3 bin). Depending on the run length, bins represent between 15 to 30 s of elution time. The returned PRMs are matched in real time to theoretical fragments of specific targets (detection).

- Upon matching a certain number of fragments in the ion trap PRM, GoDig prompts the collection of Orbitrap MS2 scans with a maximum injection time of 900 ms to accommodate weak signals. Fragment ions are matched and cosine-correlated to the library spectrum for the target peptide (identification).

- When cosine similarity is greater than 0.9 and more than 60% of the fragments with a relative abundance greater than 50% in the library spectrum are present in the experimental spectrum, GoDig selects SPS-ions that pass a fixed purity threshold and inserts a custom SPS-MS3 scan (quantification). Maximum injection time is set to 2,000 ms in order to accommodate even very weak signals.

### Data analysis of mass spectrometry data

#### Data analysis for cysteine profiling experiment and whole proteome experiments

Raw files of cysteine profiling were searched using the open-source Comet search engine (ver. 2019.01.5)49 with the Uniprot human proteome database (downloaded 11/24/2021) with contaminants and reverse decoy sequences appended. Precursor error tolerance was 50 ppm and fragment error tolerance was 0.9 m/z. Static modifications include Cys carboxyamidomethylation (+57.0215) and TMTpro18 (+304.2071) on Lys side chains and peptide N-termini. Methionine oxidation (+15.9949) and DBIA-modification on cysteine residues (+239.1628) were allowed as variable modifications. Peptide spectral matches were filtered to a peptide false discovery rate (FDR) of <1% using linear discriminant analysis employing a target-decoy strategy50,51. Resulting peptides were further filtered to obtain a 1% protein FDR at the entire dataset level (including all plexes in an experiment)52. Cysteine-modified peptides were filtered for site localization using the AScorePro algorithm with a cutoff of 13 (P < 0.05) as previously described53,54. Overlapping peptide sequences generated from different charge states, retention times and tryptic termini were grouped together into a single entry. A single quantitative value was reported, and only unique peptides were reported. Reporter ion intensities were adjusted to correct for impurities during synthesis of different TMT reagents according to the manufacturer’s specifications. For quantification of each MS3 spectrum, a total sum signal-to-noise of all reporter ions of 180 was required. Peptide quantitative values were normalized so that the sum of the signal for all proteins in each channel was equal to account for sample loading differences (column normalization).

Raw files from whole proteome analyses were processed using the same search parameters, filtering criteria, and quantification methods described for the cysteine profiling experiment. Of note, DBIA was not included as a variable modification for searches and site localization was not performed.

#### Data analysis for targeted CysDig experiments

The TMT reporter ion signals measured in each GoDig assay were extracted using the GoDig UI and exported to spreadsheets for downstream analysis in R (ver. 4.3.1) in RStudio55,56. Data formatting was performed using R/tidyverse and visualization was created using R/ggplot257,58. MS3 quantification scans for the same peptide were summed. When more than three MS3 events were triggered for the same peptide, only the top three quantification events based on numbers of fragment ions matched were kept. Column normalization was performed to correct for different protein loading in each channel. Each TMT channel was normalized using the median signal-to-noise ratio value across all the corresponding cysteines targeted within the screen. Percent compound occupancy of a given cysteine site was calculated as: Occupancy ( % ) = 100 − [ 100 × ( average compound intensity / average DMSO intensity ) ]

### Covalent docking of CL129 onto the HUWE1 active site

Docking complexes were predicted using Schrodinger Maestro Version 13.1.141, release 2022-11-3. PDB structure 3H1D4 of HUWE1 was prepared using default settings in the protein preparation wizard with a single protein chain (chain A) and ligand. Water and crystallization additives were removed and the structure underwent minimalization using default settings. Ligands were prepared using default LigPrep settings and a maximum of 32 states were generated per ligand. A box size of 20Å centered on residue 4341 was used to define the binding site. The covalent docking was conducted in pose prediction mode using Cys4341 as the reactive residue, nucleophilic substitution reaction SMARTS, a 3.5kcal/mol energy cutoff and a maximum output of 3 poses per ligand.

### Direct detection of covalent modification on the active site cysteine of HUWE1

10 μM of recombinant HUWE1 HECT domain was incubated with 50 μM of CL129 for 2 hr at room temperature. Protein was subsequently digested with trypsin for 4 hr and peptides were desalted via StageTip. CL129-adducted cysteines were searched for as a variable modification (+318.0786).

### Immunoblot analysis of CL129-treated cells

Frozen compound-treated cell pellets were lysed with RIPA buffer for 30 min at 4°C and spun down at 14,000g for 10 min at 4°C. The supernatant was collected in another tube. Approximately 15 μg of protein was resuspended in loading buffer, separated using SDS–polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis and visualized using immunoblotting. Proteins of interest were detected using the following antibodies at a dilution of 1:1,000: DDIT4 (Abcam, ab191871, rabbit), ACAT1 (Cell Signaling Technology, #44276, rabbit), β-actin (Cell Signaling Technology, #3700, mouse), β-tubulin (Cell Signaling Technology, #86298, mouse), Anti-rabbit IgG – HRP-linked (Cell Signaling Technology, #7074, goat), and Anti-mouse IgG – HRP-linked (Cell Signaling Technology, #7076, horse).

Developing new chemoproteomic platforms to decode and perturb the degradome

## Abstract

Proteins are the functional units of the cell, orchestrating virtually every biological process from

cellular metabolism and signal transduction to structural support and immune defense. The

precise and temporal regulation of protein abundance is critical to maintain cellular homeostasis

and, by extension, human health. Dysregulation of protein homeostasis can lead to many

diseases including cancer, neurodegeneration, and metabolic disorders, which highlights the

importance of understanding how exactly a protein is degraded. Doing so opens new

opportunities to therapeutically harness and reprogram protein homeostasis.

A subset of the human proteome is remarkably short-lived, with some proteins persisting for

just minutes. Despite their brief existence, these proteins play fundamental regulatory roles,

controlling key cellular processes and enabling rapid responses to external stimuli. Previous

proteomic studies from our lab using cycloheximide pulse-chase experiments have revealed that

approximately 5–10% of the human proteome consists of such short-lived proteins (SLPs).

These proteins are enriched in functionally important protein classes, including transcription

factors, ubiquitin ligases, and membrane-bound signaling receptors. Their transient nature

reflects the cell’s need to tightly regulate their abundance, often through active degradation

pathways. In a way, dissecting the mechanisms of SLP degradation provides a direct line of


<!-- Page 7 -->


iv

sight into the mind of the proteostasis network itself. The ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS)

and autophagy-lysosomal pathway (ALP) constitute a highly coordinated network of proteins

responsible for maintaining protein homeostasis through the regulated degradation and

stabilization of nearly all expressed proteins. Given their central role in cellular protein quality

control and overall cellular function, it is striking how little is known about the turnover

mechanisms of a substantial portion of the proteome. Despite these knowledge gaps, therapeutic

strategies targeting the UPS have already yielded FDA-approved drugs effective in treating

various cancers. These successes validate the UPS as a therapeutically tractable target and

underscore the importance and opportunity of understanding natural protein regulatory

mechanisms to better treat human disease. Key substrate-ligase pairs—such as NRF2-KEAP1,

HIF1A-VHL, and TP53-MDM2—serve as paradigms for how the successful decoding of how

an SLP protein is degraded can be exploited for drug development. Aside from these select few

examples, however, the precise mechanisms underlying the degradation of the overwhelming

majority of SLPs remain poorly understood. This raises fundamental questions that I sought to

answer during my PhD: through which cellular pathways are these proteins degraded? What

intrinsic features of a protein determine their specific degradation routes? Can we exploit our

SLP degradome map to identify therapeutic pinch points to target historically ‘undruggable’

proteins like transcription factors? And lastly, can we build new discovery platforms to find

molecules that precisely modulate the degradome?

Mass spectrometry–based proteomics provides a unique opportunity to capture a comprehensive

snapshot of the entire proteome in a single experiment. With chemical multiplexing using

tandem mass tag (TMT) reagents, researchers can now label and analyze up to 35 samples


<!-- Page 8 -->


v

simultaneously in one combined run. By leveraging multiplexed mass spectrometry–based

proteomics, I recognized a unique opportunity to uncover the mechanisms underlying the

degradation of hundreds of short-lived proteins (SLPs), to elucidate how the oncogenic

transcription factor ASCL1 is regulated by its endogenous ligase, and to build a complementary

drug discovery platform for identifying molecules that target the proteostasis network.

In my first project, I developed a multiplexed chemoproteomics platform to systematically

profile the degradome of a cell line of interest. This was achieved through a simple assay in

which cells were treated with potent inhibitors targeting the proteasome (Bortezomib), lysosome

(Bafilomycin A1), ubiquitin system (TAK243), neddylation system (MLN4924), and translation

machinery (cycloheximide). By quantifying protein accumulation in response to inhibitor

treatment relative to DMSO, I could determine a protein’s pathway dependencies and whether it

is short-lived in one unified proteomics-based assay. The specific patterns of accumulation in

response to these inhibitors allowed me to then categorize the short-lived proteome into

mechanistically distinct pathways. Of the SLPs that responded to chemical inhibition of the

proteostasis network, I found that proteins are either degraded by the proteasome (~70%),

lysosome (~25%), or by both pathways (~5%). Within these main degradation categories,

proteins can further be subcategorized based on their ubiquitin-dependency (ubiquitin-

dependent/CRL-independent, ubiquitin-dependent/CRL-dependent, and ubiquitin-independent).

In total, I binned proteins into 9 mechanistically distinct degradation pathways. Interestingly,

there were a subset of proteins that could not be binned into any one of the previously mentioned

categories. This was either because a protein did not meet statistical cutoffs, or more

interestingly, due to potentially being regulated by a protease or even an alternative pathway that


<!-- Page 9 -->


vi

may cause the acute depletion of these proteins. For SLPs degraded by the proteasome, I found

that virtually all these proteins are degraded in a ubiquitin-dependent manner (~95%) with a

slight bias toward non-CRL mediated degradation, which was the predominant mechanism of

degradation of most transcription factors. A small subset of proteasomal substrates (~5%) are

degraded through ubiquitin-independent mechanisms. These proteins defy the canonical model

in which substrates are first ubiquitinated and then delivered to the proteasome via shuttling

factors or through direct recognition by one of the proteasome’s many ubiquitin receptors.

Notable examples included ODC1—a pioneering case that established the concept of ubiquitin-

independent degradation by the 26S proteasome—and MIDN, a recently characterized substrate

that has reignited major interest in this degradation pathway. These ubiquitin-independent

proteasome substrates exhibit the fastest rate of degradation and are significantly smaller than

SLPs that are eliminated by other pathways. Lysosomal proteins are degraded equally in a

ubiquitin-dependent (mostly membrane-bound signaling receptors) and ubiquitin-independent

manner (mostly structural proteins). Virtually all ubiquitin-dependent lysosomal degradation

occurs in a CRL-independent manner. For proteins degraded by both pathways, the vast majority

are targeted through a ubiquitin-dependent yet CRL-independent mechanism. These substrates

are enriched at the endoplasmic reticulum, reflecting the unique mechanisms of degradation that

occur at this organelle. Overall, the findings from this atlas can inform therapeutic strategies to

modulate SLP abundance through the proteostasis network. This multiplexed degradomics assay

can be extended to include additional selective inhibitors against other key nodes of the

proteostasis network, such as heat shock proteins, p97/VCP, and specific proteasome subspecies.

Expanding the scope in this way will add granularity and resolution to our degradome map,


<!-- Page 10 -->


vii

providing deeper insight into how these short-lived yet important proteins are regulated by the

proteostasis network.

From my short-lived protein degradation atlas, I found that ASCL1 is degraded by the

proteasome in a ubiquitin-dependent, but CRL-independent manner. ASCL1 is normally a

lineage-defining master regulator of neuronal cell identity, and it drives most small cell lung

cancers (SCLCs). It is one of the deadliest cancers with limited treatment options. In close

collaboration with Dr. Keita Masuzawa from Dr. Matthew Oser’s lab, we found that ASCL1

exhibits the “Goldilocks” effect in small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) whereby levels must be

precisely maintained—too much or too little of this transcription factor are deleterious to

ASCL1-dependent SCLC cells. This suggested that there may be a therapeutic opportunity to

modulate ASCL1 levels through enhancing or inhibiting its natural turnover by its endogenous

ligase. To mechanistically dissect this regulatory axis, we employed a combination of

proteomic, functional genomics, in silico structural analysis, genetic deletion and chemical

studies. From this work, we identified that the HECT E3 ligase HUWE1 recognizes the

phosphorylated C-terminus of ASCL1 to mediate its destruction. We demonstrate that the C-

terminus is necessary for recognition and degradation by HUWE1 and conversely, we show

that this C-terminal sequence is sufficient to induce the rapid HUWE1-dependent degradation

of GFP upon transplantation. Strikingly, C-terminal mutants demonstrate increased interactions

with histones and the epigenetic machinery. This observation was corroborated via ChIP-seq

experiments. Interestingly, despite significantly prolonging ASCL1 half-life and accumulating

at canonical E-box binding motifs, C-terminal deletion mutants could not rescue survival

defects when expressed in an ASCL1 knockout background. These results suggest that the C-


<!-- Page 11 -->


viii

terminus may serve a dual role as both a potent degron and a region essential for normal

function. We performed a saturating base-editing screen to identify HUWE1 mutations that

modulate ASCL1 degradation. Charge-flipping mutations within a helix enhanced degradation,

nominating a region we term the bouncer helix. Although unresolved in prior cryo-EM

structures and predicted to be disordered, AlphaFold 3 modeling revealed that the bouncer

helix packs tightly against a positively charged pocket, termed the donut, where

phosphorylated DDIT4 was previously shown to bind. In the apo structure, the bouncer blocks

the donut, but structural modeling suggests it is displaced to permit substrate engagement. In an

orthogonal base-editing screen, we show that these bouncer helix mutations also lead to

enhanced degradation of MYCL, which we recently found to be another HUWE1 substrate

based on complementary expression proteomic and functional genomic studies. Cells

expressing these bouncer helix mutations exhibited shorter ASCL1 half-lives and enhanced

ASCL1 ubiquitination compared to WT cells. Collectively, these results reveal new druggable

interaction between the oncogenic transcription factor ASCL1 and its ligase HUWE1. We also

propose a generalizable mechanism by which HUWE1 recognizes its substrates. Lastly, we

propose that targeting molecules to the donut region of HUWE1 could enable selective gluing

and enhanced degradation of ASCL1 as a therapeutic strategy for SCLC.

For my third project, I developed a live-cell, targeted covalent drug discovery platform to

identify functional binders. Ubiquitin-mediated degradation depends on a dedicated network of

proteins that transfer ubiquitin onto substrates for proteasomal turnover. Both catalytic and

allosteric cysteines within these proteins are critical for activity, and modulating these sites can

fine-tune substrate levels. HUWE1, for example, contains a catalytic cysteine in its active site


<!-- Page 12 -->


ix

that is amenable to covalent inhibition via cysteine-targeting electrophiles. Activity-based

protein profiling (ABPP) is a powerful, unbiased approach to assess proteome-wide

electrophile reactivity. However, ABPP datasets often suffer from missing values, limiting

their utility when the goal is to find inhibitors for a specific target. To address this, I developed

CysDig, a targeted chemoproteomics platform designed to overcome the missing data problem

by enabling drug hunters to easily generate targeted proteomic assays for covalent drug

discovery. Through integration with GoDig, a TMT-based targeted proteomics strategy

developed in our lab, CysDig allows users to select up to 300 targets of interest. Unlike

conventional approaches, CysDig bypasses cysteine enrichment. In doing so, the entire

proteome remains available for quantification. Collectively, these innovations enable hybrid

targeted assays in which covalent target engagement can be measured in parallel with changes

in substrate abundance. This makes CysDig particularly well-suited for discovering small

compound engagement with UPS proteins and corresponding substrate abundance changes is

especially informative at the screening level.

Using CysDig, I identified 31 covalent inhibitors that engage the HUWE1 active site. I
