## Introduction

Historical Perspectives on Protein Degradation

For much of the 20th century, the turnover of intracellular proteins was an underappreciated

phenomenon. Many scientists assumed that most proteins, once made, were relatively long-lived,

with lysosomes, organelles filled with proteases, responsible for degrading the occasional

defective or old proteins. This view began to change in the 1970s, when studies on reticulocytes,

immature red blood cells that notably lack lysosomes, revealed the unexpected discovery that

these cells could still rapidly degrade proteins, but doing so required ATP1. In 1977, Etlinger and

Goldberg reported ATP-dependent proteolysis in reticulocyte extracts, suggesting the existence

of a new, non-lysosomal degradation machinery1. The hunt was on for this mysterious system.

By 1978, researchers found that the proteolytic activity in these extracts was not due to a single

protease but rather a complex of multiple protein components. Around the same period, ubiquitin

a small protein of then unknown function, was discovered covalently attached to histones in an

unexpected modification2. These clues all converged in the early 1980s when Avram Hershko,

Aaron Ciechanover, and Irwin Rose biochemically reconstituted a system in cell extracts where

ubiquitin was being attached to target proteins and marked them for degradation3,4. They

identified a cascade of enzymes – now known as E1, E2, and E3 – that tag proteins with

ubiquitin, and they inferred the presence of a large ATP-dependent protease that would later be

identified as the proteasome. Parallel genetic work from Alexander Varshavsky and colleagues

in yeast provided critical insights into the physiological importance of ubiquitin conjugation,

linking it to cell cycle control, stress responses, and other essential processes5–7. This set of

breakthroughs established what we now call the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS), a discovery


<!-- Page 21 -->


2

so fundamental that it earned the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2004 for Hershko, Ciechanover,

and Rose.

While the UPS story was unfolding, another protein degradation pathway known as autophagy

had been hiding in plain sight. As early as the 1950s, cell biologist Christian de Duve observed

vesicular structures consuming parts of the cell and identified the lysosome as a key degradation

organelle8. It was de Duve who coined the term autophagy (Greek for “self-eating”) in 1963 to

describe this process8. Autophagy referred to a cellular pathway in which portions of the

cytoplasm, including organelles, are sequestered into double-membraned vesicles and delivered

to lysosomes for bulk degradation. For decades, autophagy was studied largely through

morphological observations and was thought to be a non-selective, slow response to starvation or

stress. The molecular underpinnings of autophagy remained a mystery until the 1990s, when

Yoshinori Ohsumi identified genes essential for autophagy (the ATG genes) by screening for

yeast mutants defective in the process9. Ohsumi’s work, and subsequent studies in mammals10,11,

revealed that autophagy is a tightly regulated process with defined stages (initiation, vesicle

nucleation, expansion, and fusion with lysosomes) regulated by specific proteins. This

renaissance in autophagy research led to Ohsumi being awarded the Nobel Prize in Physiology

for Medicine in 2016.

The discovery of the UPS and the autophagy-lysosome pathway (ALP) dramatically changed our

perception of cellular protein homeostasis. Instead of proteins simply accumulating until diluted

by cell division or removed by passive lysosomal house-cleaning, we now appreciate a highly

orchestrated proteostasis network. This network manages protein levels through dedicated

machinery that can either selectively destroys individual proteins or engulfs bulk cellular


<!-- Page 22 -->


3

material12. The foundation was then set for scientists to dissect how these systems function, how

they intersect, and how they could be harnessed for therapeutic gain.

The Ubiquitin-Proteasome System (UPS): Anatomy and Function

At the heart of the UPS is the 26S proteasome, a massive ~2.5 MDa protein complex acting as a

molecular shredder of proteins13. It consists of a cylindrical 20S core particle and one or two 19S

regulatory particles attached at its ends, forming a dumbbell-like structure. The 20S core is a

stack of four rings (each ring composed of seven protein subunits) that assemble into a barrel.

Other regulatory ‘hats’ can be worn and other subspecies of 20S proteasomes are assembled in

specific cell types, such as the thymus and immune cells. The inner two rings are made of β

subunits that harbor protease active sites on the inside face of the barrel, creating an enclosed

degradation chamber. These active sites are threonine proteases that perform peptide bond

hydrolysis. The end rings are composed of α subunits that form a gate via N-terminal tails that

control access to the chamber. Substrates cannot enter the core unless this gate is opened by the

binding of a 19S particle14,15.

The 19S regulatory particle plays several crucial roles. For example, it recognizes polyubiquitin

chains on protein substrates often through dedicated ubiquitin receptors such as Rpn1/PSMD2,

Rpn10/PSMD4 and Rpn13/ADRM1. The 19S regulatory particle uses its ATPase subunits in the

base to unfold ubiquitylated protein substrates and to open the α-ring gate of the 20S core,

thereby translocating the unfolded polypeptide into the proteolytic chamber. Within the core, six

total proteolytic active sites each with specific substrate preferences cut the translocated substrate

into short peptides. Those peptides are then released and further broken down by other


<!-- Page 23 -->


4

peptidases16, presented on the cell surface upon being loaded onto MHC-complexes17, or even

play roles in signaling18 or the innate immune response19.

Canonical targeting of a substrate to the proteasome requires prior ubiquitination of the substrate.

Ubiquitin is a small 76-amino acid protein that can be covalently attached via its C-terminal

glycine to lysine residues on target proteins. This reaction occurs through an enzymatic cascade4.

First, an E1 ubiquitin-activating enzyme uses ATP to form a high-energy thioester with

ubiquitin, then ubiquitin is transferred to an E2 ubiquitin-conjugating enzyme, and finally, an E3

ubiquitin ligase mediates the transfer of ubiquitin from the E2 or from the E3 itself to the

substrate protein. E3 ligases are the reason why the UPS can exert such remarkable specificity

toward a defined subset of substrates – with over 600 E3s encoded in the human genome, each

recognizes substrate sequence or structural motifs20. These features are called degrons as initially

described by Varshavsky and colleagues21. Usually, substrates receive not just a single ubiquitin,

but a whole chain of ubiquitin molecules linked typically through Lys48 (K48) of ubiquitin.

These K48-linked polyubiquitin chains are especially effective at targeting proteins to the

proteasome by binding ubiquitin receptors on the19S lid22,23. The complex architecture of

ubiquitin chains and their roles within the cell are entire fields in of themselves and are reviewed

in depth in the following reviews24,25. Once a substrate is polyubiquitinated, it is engaged either

by shuttle proteins that escort the protein to the proteasome or directly by the 19S regulatory

particle26,27. Efficient degradation often requires an unstructured tail or initiation region on the

substrate to begin unfolding. As the protein is threaded into the proteasome, its ubiquitin chains

are removed by deubiquitinating enzymes (DUBs), allowing ubiquitin to be recycled and

potentially allowing the escape of the substrate from the proteasome28. This creates a molecular

race between life and death, underscoring the extensive regulation that occurs at the proteasome.


<!-- Page 24 -->


5

While ubiquitin-dependent proteasomal degradation has been discussed above, rules are meant to

be broken. A handful of proteasome substrates have been shown to undergo ubiquitin-

independent degradation. One of the earliest and best-characterized examples is ornithine

decarboxylase (ODC1), the rate-limiting enzyme in polyamine biosynthesis. ODC1 is degraded

directly by the 26S proteasome without ubiquitin modification, but instead through binding to its

regulatory protein antizyme (OAZ1). Antizyme binding induces conformational changes in

ODC1 that expose a ubiquitin-independent degron, enabling direct recognition by the

proteasome29,30. More recently, interest in this pathway has resurged with studies on MIDN, an

adaptor protein that facilitates the ubiquitin-independent degradation of its substrates by

essentially acting as the proteasome’s “hand,” capturing substrates for turnover31. These findings

raise important questions: Are there additional proteins that bypass ubiquitination, and to what

extent does MIDN contribute to their degradation? In Chapter 2, I will discuss my discovery of

dozens of novel ubiquitin-independent proteasome substrates.

In summary, the UPS is a selective and highly regulated degradation route. Proteins are marked

with the ‘kiss of death’ in the form of ubiquitin (or not) and then executed by the proteasome.

This system regulates many critical processes in the cell. For example, cell cycle transitions are

driven by the timed destruction of cyclins and other regulators via ubiquitin ligases such as the

APC/C and SCF complexes32,33. Misfolded or damaged proteins are recognized and removed to

maintain protein quality control34,35. Numerous signaling pathways are modulated by regulated

turnover of transcription factors and kinases, reflecting how the UPS shapes cellular

signaling33,36. Given its central role, it is no surprise that the UPS is tightly controlled and

integrated with other cellular systems such as the transcriptional machinery and its counterpart,

the autophagy-lysosome pathway (ALP).


<!-- Page 25 -->


6

The Autophagy-Lysosome Pathway (ALP): Anatomy and Function

Autophagy is a complementary degradation system to the UPS, specialized for handling large or

heterogeneous cargo37. In macroautophagy, cellular material is traditionally sequestered within a

double-membraned phagophore that expands and closes to form an autophagosome, typically

500–1000 nm in diameter38. These vesicles are thought to encapsulate cytosolic components

such as long-lived proteins, aggregates, damaged organelles such as mitochondria, or even

invading microbes. Autophagosomes move along cytoskeletal tracks and fuse with lysosomes,

where the acidic, enzyme-rich environment degrades the cargo into amino acids, fatty acids, and

sugars that are recycled for biosynthesis and energy39.

The autophagy pathway is orchestrated by a whole host of ATG proteins. In mammals, initiation

is controlled by the ULK1 kinase complex, which integrates upstream signals from mTORC1

and AMPK to activate or suppress autophagy depending on nutrient and energy status40,41.

Following initiation, nucleation of the phagophore is driven by a class III phosphatidylinositol 3-

kinase complex composed of Beclin 1, ATG14, and Vps3442,43. During phagophore expansion,

two ubiquitin-like conjugation systems operate: one that conjugates ATG12 to ATG5, and

another that lipidates LC3/ATG8 to decorate the autophagosomal membrane44–46. Finally,

closure and fusion with lysosomes are mediated by SNARE proteins and the HOPS complex,

which drive membrane fusion to form the autolysosome47.

Although autophagy is traditionally seen as a non-selective process, it can also be a highly

selective one48. Cargo adaptors such as p62/SQSTM1, NBR1, and CALCOCO2 recognize

ubiquitinated substrates and simultaneously bind LC3, linking protein aggregates or defective

organelles to the forming autophagosome48. In this way, ubiquitin can similarly function as a tag


<!-- Page 26 -->


7

for autophagic clearance. Once cargo is degraded, permeases and transporters in the lysosomal

membrane export the breakdown products back to the cytosol49,50. In sum, the ALP is an

indispensable system for nutrient recycling, organelle turnover, and cellular quality control,

particularly during starvation, differentiation, and in conditions characterized by protein

aggregation or organelle damage.

Crosstalk Between the UPS and Autophagy

For many years, the UPS and autophagy were viewed as separate systems with one degrading

individual proteins, the other handling bulk material. While the substrate specificities of each

system may be distinct, these two degradation systems are now recognized as interconnected

arms of an integrated proteolytic network that cooperate to maintain proteostasis51,52. A central

point of intersection is ubiquitin. While K48-linked chains mark proteins for proteasomal

degradation, K63-linked chains often signal for autophagy via adaptor proteins such as p62,

which connect ubiquitinated aggregates or organelles to autophagosomes53,54. Thus, ubiquitin

functions as a shared code that helps cells allocate substrates between the two pathways.

The systems also compensate for each other. Proteasome inhibition, for example by bortezomib,

triggers the upregulation of autophagy to relieve proteotoxic stress, while blockade of autophagy

can increase reliance on the UPS55–57. In neurodegenerative models, where aggregates

overwhelm the proteasome, enhancing autophagy provides relief58,59. Regulatory factors help

coordinate this balance. For example, mTORC1 suppresses autophagy under nutrient sufficiency

while promoting protein synthesis and elevating UPS demand; conversely, its inhibition during

starvation shifts the burden toward autophagy60,61. Likewise, the transcription factor NFE2L1 is

activated upon proteasome stress, translocates to the nucleus to upregulate proteasome subunit


<!-- Page 27 -->


8

genes and has also been shown to activate autophagy-related gene programs62,63. Many substrates

can be handled by either system64–66. Aggregates resistant to proteasomal degradation, for

instance, are cleared through aggrephagy, where p62 both binds ubiquitinated aggregates and

oligomerizes to tether them to autophagosomes. In this way, the UPS and autophagy form a

cooperative continuum rather than operate in isolation. Their crosstalk ensures that if one

pathway is impaired, the other can compensate.

The Proteostasis Network as a Therapeutic Target

Dysregulation of protein degradation underlies many diseases. In cancer, oncoproteins can

accumulate due to stabilizing mutations or via gene amplifications that lead to their

overproduction67,68. In neurodegenerative disorders, defective clearance of misfolded proteins

leads to toxic aggregates69. Pathogens like viruses hijack can hijack the host’s degradation

machinery to evade immune responses70. Given the undeniable centrality of protein degradation

to cellular function and its dysregulation as a driver of human disease, it is perhaps no surprise

that the proteostasis network has become an important and validated target for drug

development71. Proteostasis-targeting therapeutic strategies can be broadly grouped into three

categories. The first consists of global modulators that act on key arms of the proteostasis

network, broadly influencing protein folding, degradation, or quality control. The second

includes selective hijackers that repurpose specific components of the system to direct the fate of

a chosen target. The third encompasses precision modulators that fine-tune the abundance of an

individual protein by exploiting endogenous regulatory mechanisms.

Category 1: Global inhibitors of key nodes (proteasome inhibitors and more)


<!-- Page 28 -->


9

Bortezomib (Velcade®), a boronic acid peptide that reversibly inhibits the proteasome’s

chymotrypsin-like activity, was approved in 2003 for the treatment of multiple myeloma72. This

landmark approval represented the first FDA-approved drug deliberately designed to target the

ubiquitin-proteasome pathway. By blocking the proteasome, bortezomib causes an accumulation

of proteins, especially misfolded or abnormal proteins, in myeloma cells, triggering stress and

apoptosis73. Following bortezomib’s success, second-generation proteasome inhibitors were

developed such as carfilzomib (Kyprolis®, an epoxyketone that irreversibly inhibits proteasome

active sites) and ixazomib (Ninlaro®, an orally available boronate)74,75. However, their broad

mechanism of action coupled to the ubiquitous expression of proteasomes in virtually all cells

leads to unwanted side effects such as peripheral neuropathy and gastrointestinal issues76,

limiting therapeutic efficacy. This has spurred interest in more selective modulators of the

proteostasis machinery such as p97/VCP inhibitors or heat shock protein inhibitors77,78.

Category 2: Hijacking components of the proteostasis network for therapeutic gain

(PROTACs/iMIDs)

The second generation of proteostasis-targeting therapies marked a significant paradigm shift.

Instead of globally inhibiting degradation machinery, these approaches enhance the degradation

of a specific protein by hijacking the proteostasis machinery. Rather than inhibiting a protein’s

function with a traditional occupancy-based inhibitor, these methods eliminate the protein

outright, which is a fundamentally different mode of action that may overcome traditional drug

resistance mechanisms. Conceptualized in the early 2000s and first demonstrated by Ray

Deshaies and Craig Crews, PROTACs (PROteolysis TArgeting Chimeras) exemplify this

technology79. These Frankenstein-like bifunctional molecules link a target protein to an E3


<!-- Page 29 -->


10

ubiquitin ligase, inducing ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation. Several

PROTACs have entered clinical trials and have demonstrated therapeutic efficacy80. Small

molecule molecular glues similarly facilitate an interaction between a target and an E3 ligase

while possessing more drug-like properties than their bifunctional counterparts. Notably,

immunomodulatory drugs (IMiDs) such as thalidomide, lenalidomide, and pomalidomide

(originally developed as a sedative) were later discovered to act as molecular glues that possess

potent antimyeloma activity. By binding the CRL4CRBN (cereblon) E3 ligase and promoting neo-

interactions with the transcription factors IKZF1 and IKZF3, they induce ubiquitination and

proteasomal degradation of these factors81,82. In retrospect, lenalidomide acted as a molecular

glue long before the term existed and its mechanism was understood, serving as early proof that

hijacking the proteostasis network could become a cornerstone of modern medicine.

Beyond PROTACs and glues, the field has blossomed to include many other proximity-inducing

modalities and, of course, their corresponding acronyms. LYTACs (lysosome-targeting

chimeras) direct extracellular proteins to lysosomal receptors for endocytosis and degradation,

while AUTACs and ATTECs tag cytosolic cargo for autophagic clearance83,84. Conversely,

targeted protein stabilization represents the flip side of degradation. DUBTACs (DeUBiquitinase

TArgeting Chimeras) recruit deubiquitinases to remove ubiquitin from specific substrates,

thereby rescuing proteins from turnover. This strategy has been used to stabilize proteins such as

CFTR, offering therapeutic promise in diseases like cystic fibrosis. Together, these approaches

highlight how induced proximity has become a versatile framework for controlling protein fate

in cells via the proteostasis network.

Category 3: Precision medicines targeting endogenous protein regulatory mechanisms


<!-- Page 30 -->


11

A third generation of strategies targeting the proteostasis machinery has begun to pick up

momentum. By understanding the endogenous turnover mechanisms of a protein, it is possible to

then develop rational strategies to fine-tune protein abundance in a precise manner. In the case of

protein stabilization, many cancers overproduce the E3 ligase MDM2, which suppresses the

tumor suppressor p53 by driving its degradation. Small molecules such as Nutlin-3a disrupt the

MDM2–p53 interaction, thereby stabilizing p53 and restoring its tumor-killing activity at this

well-characterized protein–protein interface.85 Conversely, as a striking example of targeted

degradation via allostery, Vividion’s covalent molecular glue VVD-065 binds KEAP1 at

Cys151, which allosterically enhances its interaction with CUL3, thereby accelerating

degradation of its natural substrate NRF2/NFE2L286. Another illustrative case is seen with β-

catenin (CTNNB1) and β-TrCP (BTRC), whereby molecular glue compounds were found to

reestablish or enhance the natural interaction between phosphomutant β-catenin and its E3 ligase

β-TrCP87.

In summary, we can classify proteostasis-targeting therapeutics into three waves: (1) broad and

non-selective inhibitors of protein synthesis, folding, or degradation machinery (proteasome,

lysosome, heat shock protein inhibitors) (2) targeted protein degraders and other induced

proximity tools – highly selective removal of chosen targets through hijacking endogenous

cellular machinery; (3) precise fine-tuning of intrinsic degradation pathways – either enhancing

or blocking specific protein interactions. As we deepen our mechanistic understanding of how

each protein is degraded, we will be better able to pharmacologically modulate them with

increasing precision.

The Need to Systematically Decode the Cellular Degradome


<!-- Page 31 -->


12

Successful decoding of endogenous protein regulatory mechanisms by the proteostasis network

have led to small molecule therapies now being tested in clinical trials71. A systematic effort to

decode how proteins are degraded would therefore accelerate translational endeavors and

strategies to treat multiple diseases. Unfortunately, we still don’t fully understand how each

protein is turned over, nor which components of the proteostasis machinery are responsible for

degrading which specific proteins. In other words, a degradation map of the cell, the degradome,

remains grossly incomplete. This is not surprising as mapping the degradome is not trivial. The

proteostasis network is immensely complex. As previously mentioned, there are hundreds of E3,

dozens of DUBs, and many autophagy receptors, each potentially acting on a subset of

substrates, sometimes redundantly or in a conditional manner88,89. Given this complexity, it’s

understandable why a complete map has not been achieved yet. But it’s also increasingly clear

that without efforts toward such a map, we will miss opportunities to fully decipher the

regulatory logic of the proteostasis network that would inform new therapeutic strategies for

intervention.

Technologies for Decoding the Degradome

How can we systematically map protein degradation pathways? Traditional biochemistry and

cell biology provides deep mechanistic insight into one protein at a time. While invaluable, such

approaches are low-throughput if the goal is to systematically study a substantial portion of the

degradome. In recent years, researchers have developed high-throughput genetic platforms to

tackle this challenge.

One pioneering approach was developed by Stephen Elledge and colleagues and is known as

Global Protein Stability (GPS) profiling89–94. The core of GPS is a genetically encoded reporter


<!-- Page 32 -->


13

system that fuses a peptide or protein of interest to a fluorescent reporter like GFP along with an

internal reference fluorescent protein like RFP. The ratio of GFP to RFP in a cell reflects the

stability of the fused substrate. Unstable substrates yield low GFP/RFP ratios because GFP gets

degraded along with the fusion, whereas stable substrates accumulate and give higher ratios.

Elledge’s team used this system to identify what proteins or peptides are dependent on the cullin-

ring ligase (CRL) system90,91,93.

However, genetic approaches like GPS have their limitations. Because they rely on exogenously

expressed fusion proteins, they might not faithfully recapitulate the behavior of a protein in its

native context, or the exogenous overexpression of a protein may overwhelm endogenous

regulatory mechanisms. Additionally, these genetically encoded libraries, in their current form,

do not encapsulate the whole proteome and so new libraries must be synthesized, which is costly

and labor intensive. Equally powerful and complementary approaches that can systematically

study the native proteome are needed.

Enter proteomics. Advances in mass spectrometry make it possible to measure protein levels and

turnover on a proteome-wide scale and at unprecedented depth. One strategy to profile the

degradome is to perform pulse-chase experiments and measure the decay of proteins directly

either using SILAC-labeling to study medium to long-lived proteins or cycloheximide to study

short-lived proteins95–97. This kind of proteome-wide approach captures proteins in their native

state, with all their endogenous post-translational modifications and interactions that might affect

stability.

Short-lived Proteins: Important Regulatory Proteins that Undergo Active Degradation


<!-- Page 33 -->


14

Short-lived proteins undergo constitutive and rapid turnover (half-lives spanning hours at most),

implying that they possess inherent features that make them more likely to be acutely degraded

by the proteostasis network97. SLPs tend to be the cell’s master regulators and responders as they

are enriched in transcription factors, signaling molecules, cell cycle proteins, oncogenes, and

tumor suppressors. Their dynamic regulation ensures that protein levels can be tuned quickly by

synthesis and degradation, allowing the cell to appropriately respond as needed. Thus, by

studying how SLPs are destroyed, we can glean direct insights into the mind of the proteostasis

network. From a therapeutic standpoint, this understanding can be harnessed to develop new

strategies for targeting proteins traditionally considered “undruggable,” such as transcription

factors including MYC, NRF2/NFEL2, and CTNNB198.

In a study led by Dr. Jiaming Li from our lab, she treated cells with cycloheximide and used 16-

plex TMT labeling reagents to quantify protein levels at numerous time points in four different

human cell lines97. With this approach, the team directly measured degradation kinetics for over

11,000 proteins, identifying about 1,017 proteins as short-lived (half-life ≤ 8 hrs). This dataset

revealed the identity of the human short-lived proteome. These proteins tended to be lower in

abundance, are often evolutionarily younger, and are less thermally stable on average than long-

lived proteins. This work brought forward an obvious question that I decided to answer as part of

my PhD work. By what mechanisms are these SLPs acutely depleted? This is further explored in

the first half of Chapter 2 where I developed a new chemoproteomics assay to classify the short-

lived proteome into mechanistically distinct pathways.

ASCL1: A Genetically Validated Therapeutic Target for the Majority of Small Cell Lung

Cancers (SCLCs)


<!-- Page 34 -->


15

In the latter half of Chapter 2, I demonstrate how the degradome atlas resource can inform the

successful decoding of a therapeutically relevant protein, ASCL1. Small cell lung cancer (SCLC)

is an aggressive neuroendocrine cancer characterized by loss of RB1 and TP53 and lacking

recurrent oncogenic driver mutations99. Instead, it comprises molecular subtypes defined by

lineage transcription factors: ASCL1 (~60%), NEUROD1 (~20%), and POU2F3 (~10%)99.

These factors often act as lineage dependencies, with genetic studies showing ASCL1 is required

for tumor growth in mouse models and ASCL1-positive cancer cell lines, including some

neuroblastomas100. Despite its clear role as a therapeutic target, ASCL1 is difficult to drug due to

the absence of ligand-binding pockets98.

ASCL1 is a basic helix–loop–helix (bHLH) transcription factor expressed in SCLC and during

neural development, where it binds E-box partners such as TCF3, TCF4, and TCF12 to drive

transcription101. In SCLC, ASCL1 directly activates oncogenic programs including MYCL,

SOX2, and DLL3, which is the target of Tarlatamab, a DLL3-directed bispecific T-cell engager

recently approved for second-line SCLC treatment102. While ASCL1 is broadly required in

neural development, its expression in adult tissues is limited, supporting its potential as a

selective therapeutic target in ASCL1-dependent cancers103.

One strategy to target lineage transcription factors is by modulating their stability. ASCL1 is a

short-lived protein regulated by the E3 ligase HUWE1 during neural development, where

HUWE1-mediated degradation promotes neural stem cell quiescence104. HUWE1 has also been

linked to ASCL1 turnover in SCLC, though the underlying mechanisms remain unclear105,106.

Given ASCL1’s role as a lineage dependency and regulator of oncogenic programs including

DLL3, we set out to systematically identify mechanisms controlling its expression and stability.


<!-- Page 35 -->


16

To do so, we performed genome-wide CRISPR knockout and base editor screens with

endogenous ASCL1 abundance reporters in an ASCL1⁺, ASCL1-dependent SCLC model. Our

collective studies reveal how ASCL1 is degraded by its ligase, HUWE1, and importantly, inform

new strategies for the targeted degradation of this transcription factor.

Proteomics Enables the Proteome-Wide Study and Discovery of Small Molecule Ligands

So what does one do once a target and therapeutic strategy has been identified? Mass

spectrometry-based proteomics has emerged as a promising method of choice for drug discovery,

enabling researchers to discover and characterize ligand-protein interactions at proteome-wide

scale107–109. Among the available proteomic methods, activity-based protein profiling (ABPP)

has been especially impactful in covalent drug discovery. This technique enables the mapping of

covalent small-molecule binding to the entire cysteinome. With advances in multiplexing and

streamlined workflows from our lab, ABPP is now a high-throughput platform that enables the

rapid screening of covalent molecule libraries against the cysteinome109,110. The application of

this platform to find ligands targeting the proteostasis network is especially powerful since

cysteines are critical for ubiquitin transfer and enzymatic activity.

The Utility of Applying Targeted Proteomic Workflows for Covalent Drug Discovery

An important consideration in proteomics is the tradeoff between unbiased, discovery-driven

approaches and targeted methods. Unbiased data acquisition strategies can reveal unexpected

biology but often suffer from missing values across experiments, leading to false negatives and

wasted effort. Targeted proteomics, by contrast, offers consistent quantification and deeper

coverage for proteins of interest111. Motivated by repeatedly missing key targets in my own


<!-- Page 36 -->


17

cysteine profiling experiments, I developed a new targeted chemoproteomic platform called

CysDig (Chapter 3) that integrates covalent ligand profiling with targeted mass spectrometry-

based workflows112. Of note, this screening platform enables dual readouts that capture both

compound engagement and protein abundance in a single unified assay, directly linking binding

events to functional protein abundance changes.

The research presented in this thesis is organized into two main chapters, both of which revolve

around a unifying vision: systematic decoding of the degradome can fuel fundamental biological

and therapeutic insights. In Chapter 2, I provided the community with a comprehensive map of

the short-lived protein degradome. Building on this resource, I teamed up with Dr. Matthew

Oser’s lab to dissect the regulation of ASCL1, a lineage-defining transcription factor and

attractive therapeutic target for SCLC. Our work illustrates how understanding the mechanisms

of protein degradation in detail can reveal new actionable therapeutic strategies for otherwise

elusive targets such as transcription factors. In Chapter 3, I present a targeted chemoproteomic

discovery platform designed to identify covalent binders with minimal missing values while

simultaneously quantifying protein abundance in the same assay. Using this platform, I discover

and characterize a molecule that covalently binds to the active site of the HECT E3 ligase,

HUWE1.

Chapter 2.1: Introduction

Proteostasis is dynamically maintained through tightly regulated protein degradation pathways,

with the ubiquitin-proteasome system (UPS) and the autophagy-lysosomal pathway

(ALP) serving as the two principal mechanisms of intracellular proteolysis12,52. These systems

are critical for the selective elimination of proteins to regulate signaling networks, remove

damaged or misfolded proteins, and adapt to cellular stress. While the transcriptional regulation

of gene expression has been extensively characterized, posttranslational mechanisms governing

protein stability remain less well understood, despite the central role of protein degradation in

nearly every aspect of cellular function

In the UPS, substrate proteins are marked for degradation by a hierarchical cascade of ubiquitin-

conjugating enzymes, culminating in the conjugation of ubiquitin to lysine residues on target

proteins. Polyubiquitinated proteins are then recognized and degraded by the 26S proteasome,

ensuring precise control over protein abundance and function. However, accumulating evidence

indicates that a subset of proteasomal substrates undergoes ubiquitin-independent degradation,

highlighting alternative proteasomal targeting mechanisms30,31. In contrast, the autophagy-

lysosomal system mediates the bulk degradation of cytoplasmic components, including protein

aggregates and organelles, via vesicular trafficking to the lysosome37.

A recent proteomic study identified the short-lived proteome, but the mechanisms of their acute

depletion remain poorly understood97. To dissect the molecular logic governing these pathways, I

applied multiplexed proteomics in combination with potent and selective pharmacological


<!-- Page 40 -->


21

inhibitors targeting key nodes of both the UPS and autophagy. This approach allowed me to

systematically classify hundreds of proteins based on their degradation dependencies into 9

mechanistically distinct degradation mechanisms. Importantly, this study reveals the regulatory

logic of how the proteostasis network degrades the short-lived proteome and provides a valuable

resource for targeted protein degradation and stabilization applications.

To follow-up on enabling insights gleaned from our degradome map, I further investigated the

post-translational regulation of ASCL1 by the ubiquitin-proteasome system in close

collaboration with Dr. Keita Masuzawa from Dr. Matt Oser’s lab. ASCL1 drives most small cell

lung cancers (SCLCs) and is an attractive therapeutic target. However, its lack of canonical drug

binding pockets makes it an elusive target. Through decoding how ASCL1 is degraded by its

endogenous ligase, HUWE1, we suggest new therapeutic strategies for its targeted degradation.

Chapter 2.2: A multiplexed chemoproteomics strategy to dissect the short-lived protein

degradome in human cells

Cycloheximide pulse-chase assays coupled to a mass spectrometry-based enables the proteome-

wide identification of short-lived proteins and the ability to simultaneously ascribe half-life

estimates. A previous report identified hundreds of these short-lived proteins, however, the

mechanisms of their acute depletion remained largely unknown (Figure 2.1A), motivating my

interest in developing a platform that could bin the short-lived degradome into distinct

degradation pathways. To reveal the short-lived degradome in human cells, I used TMT-pro

18plex reagents coupled to potent and selective inhibitors of distinct nodes of the proteostasis

network (Figure 2.1B). These inhibitors included BTZ (proteasome inhibitor), Bafilomycin A1

(lysosome inhibitor), TAK243 (ubiquitination inhibitor), MLN4924 (neddylation inhibitor), and

CHX (translation inhibitor). The idea was that, in one simple and unified mass spectrometry-

based assay, we could determine pathway dependencies of a given protein, and the patterns of

those dependences would then inform on their specific mechanism of degradation. (Figure

2.1B). For example, CDC25A is an important phosphatase that regulates the cell cycle and it is

known to be degraded by the APC/C complex113. As a positive control, we highlight its relative

abundance changes across upon chemical inhibition across all four probed cell lines (Figure

2.1C). CDC25A accumulates upon proteasome inhibition, ubiquitination inhibition, CRL-

inhibition and is acutely depleted upon CHX treatment. Together, we can say that CDC25A is a

short-lived protein that is degraded in a proteasome-dependent, ubiquitin-dependent, and CRL-

dependent manner. Because of the proteome-wide readouts that are attained from this assay, we

were able to systematically classify the short-lived proteome into unique degradation

mechanisms.

Chapter 2.3: An overview of short-lived proteins degraded by the proteasome, lysosome, or

by both pathways

Of the SLPs (defined as decreasing by at least 1.5 fold relative to DMSO with an adjusted p-

value less than or equal to .05) that increased in abundance by either proteasomal or lysosomal

inhibition (defined as at least a 1.2 fold change relative to DMSO), we see that the proteasome

degrades most SLPs (~70%), followed by the lysosome (~25%), and lastly a small subset of the

short-lived proteome is degraded by both pathways (~5%) (Figure 2.2A-D). We found that SH-

SY5Y cells possessed the lowest number of short-lived proteins, despite quantifying a similar

number of total proteins across all lines (~10,000 proteins). This could be because these cells

divide at a much slower rate compared to the other cell lines with a reported doubling time of

about 50 hrs. Looking at the ubiquitin dependency across these three main degradation pathways,

we found that virtually all proteasomal degradation occurs in a ubiquitin dependent manner with

the interesting observation of a small subset degraded in a ubiquitin-independent manner (Figure

2.2E-I). Among lysosomal substrates, we found a slightly higher number of substrates degraded

in ubiquitin-independent than in a ubiquitin-dependent manner (Figures 2E-I). Of the small

percentage of proteins found to be degraded by both the proteasome and lysosome, we found that

most proteins are degraded in a ubiquitin-dependent manner (Figures 2E-I).


<!-- Page 44 -->


25

Within the cell, proteasomal substrates were found to be enriched in the nucleus, cytoplasm,

midbody, and cilium. Lysosomal substrates were enriched in the plasma membrane, vesicle,

extracellular exosome, and endoplasmic reticulum lumen. Proteins degraded by both pathways

were found to be enriched in the endoplasmic reticulum membrane, which makes sense as

proteins at the ER can undergo both ERphagy or ERAD (Figure 2.2J).

Functionally, proteasome substrates regulate transcription, chromatin binding, play roles in the

transfer of ubiquitin onto substrates, and exhibit protein kinase activity. Lysosomal substrates

exhibit transmembrane signaling receptor activity, growth factor binding, endopeptidase activity,

and integrin binding. Substrates degraded by both pathways exhibit oxidoreductase activity

(Figure 2.2K).

The proteasome regulates transcription by RNA polymerase II, the cell cycle, DNA damage

response, and chromosome segregation. Functionally, lysosomal substrates mediate processes

such as cell adhesion, cell migration, cell-cell signaling, and organismal growth. (Figure 2.2L).

No significant biological processes were enriched for proteins degraded by both pathways.

Chapter 2.4: The short-lived proteome can be further stratified based on ubiquitin

dependency

Short-lived proteins can be further stratified based on their ubiquitin dependency. Proteins that

accumulate upon the chemical inhibition of the ubiquitin machinery via TAK243 can be defined

as ubiquitin-dependent. Within the UPS, a dedicated system of E3 ligases known as cullin-ring

ligases can be chemically inactivated with MLN4924, a neddylation inhibitor. Therefore,

proteins that were found to undergo ubiquitin-dependent degradation can further be

subcategorized as CRL-dependent or not. With this classification logic, we grouped proteins into

9 possible degradation categories.


<!-- Page 47 -->


28

As mentioned earlier, proteasomal degradation occurs mostly in a ubiquitin-dependent manner

with a slight bias toward CRL-independent degradation (Figures 2.3A-C). We noticed that the

abundances of transcription factors are regulated mostly in a ubiquitin-dependent manner, which

will be touched upon in the next chapter. Of note, we discover dozens of new proteasome-

dependent, ubiquitin-independent substrates (Figure 2.3A). Positive controls included ODC1,

MIDN, and AKIRIN2. Ubiquitin-dependent, but CRL-independent proteasomal degradation of

short-lived proteins included known proteins such as MCL1 (ubiquitinated by HUWE1),

EIF2AK1 (ubiquitinated by UBR4), and TP53 (ubiquitinated by MDM2) (Figure 2.3B). Many

known E3 substrate receptors (APPBP2, BTBD1, BTRC, CCNF, DCAF15, DTL, FBXO11,

FEM1A, KBTB7, SOCS4, SPOP), substrates of CRL E3 ligases (BACH1, CRY1/2, EID1,

FNIP1, HES1, MYC, NUSAP1, PDCD4, and RIT1), and cell cycle proteins (CCND1, CCND2,

CCND3, CCNE2, CDK4, CDC6, CDT1) appear as proteasome-dependent, ubiquitin-dependent,

and CRL-dependent substrates, bolstering the confidence in our approach to accurately bin the

short-lived protein degradome (Figure 2.3C).

Lysosome-dependent degradation occurs in a mostly ubiquitin-independent manner (Figures

2.3D-F). Substrates that undergo this route of degradation play key roles in integrin binding

(ITGBL1, TSPAN4, and CD151) and in maintaining the structural composition of the

extracellular matrix (ECM1, COL6A2, and COL5A1). Lysosomal proteins that are degraded in a

ubiquitin-dependent, but CRL-independent manner are involved in transmembrane signaling

(TNFRSF1A, RET, ACVR2B and BMPR1A) (Figure 2.3D) and transmembrane transporter

activity (SLC4A2, SLC38A2, and ZDHHC13) (Figure 2.3E). We found a small number of

proteins degraded by the lysosome in a ubiquitin-dependent and CRL-dependent manner (FZD7,


<!-- Page 48 -->


29

FAU, and PCDHAC2) (Figure 2.3F). This finding likely reflects the fact that CRL E3 ligases

have mostly evolved to degrade intracellular proteins or may not be largely involved in the

lysosomal-dependent degradation of short-lived proteins.

The most uncommon form of short-lived protein degradation involved proteins degraded by both

the proteasome and the lysosome. Most proteins that are degraded by both pathways are

destroyed in a ubiquitin-dependent, but CRL-independent manner (Figures 2.3G-I). Examples

include PINK1, KLHL24, NCOA4, IREB2, and PLEKHB2 (Figure 2.3H). Proteins degraded by

both systems in a ubiquitin-dependent and CRL-dependent manner include KLF11, RNF19B,

and PDCD4 (Figure 2.3I). The degradation of these proteins by both systems may indicate that

these proteins may have context-dependent roles within the cell and that they may require

different modes of degradation as a result.

Chapter 2.5: Proteasome-dependent and ubiquitin-dependent control of transcription

factor abundance

Transcription factors are master regulators of the cell, quickly integrating extracellular signals to

dynamically initiate or repress transcriptional programs that enable the cell to respond to its

environment or to change its state. Dysregulation of transcription factor activity is implicated in

many human diseases so understanding the mechanisms regulating their stability offers new

therapeutic strategies especially since these proteins lack canonical small molecule binding

pockets.

From our dataset, we found that almost all TFs found to be short-lived are degraded by the

proteasome (Figure 2.4A). Virtually all transcription factors are degraded in a ubiquitin-

dependent manner with a higher number of these TFs degraded in a CRL-independent manner

(Figure 2.4B). C2H2 zinc finger-containing transcription factors were the most abundant type of

transcription factor found to be regulated by the UPS, albeit they comprise the largest family of

transcription factors (Figure 2.4C). As four representative examples of proteasome-dependent,


<!-- Page 51 -->


32

ubiquitin-dependent, but CRL-independent degradation, we showcase SOX4, SREBF1, ASCL1,

and MYB (Figure 2.4D-G). As four representative examples of proteasome-dependent,

ubiquitin-dependent, and CRL-dependent degradation, we showcase BACH1, CEBPB, NFE2L2,

and KLF7 (Figure 2.4H-K) Each of these transcription factors play fundamental roles in the cell

from driving leukemias in the case of MYB, controlling cholesterol homeostasis in the case of

SREBF1, to defining neuronal cell identify in the case of ASCL1. The resource presented here

gives a proteome-wide overview of how exactly these master regulators are disposed of by the

proteostasis network. To demonstrate that deep decoding of the degradome can lead to new

therapeutic strategies, we followed up with understanding how ASCL1 is degraded by its ligase.

Chapter 2.7: Identification of the C-terminus of ASCL1 as a degron

Using AlphaFold 2 multimer, we broke down human HUWE1 into 9 pieces (due to the

computational limitations of ColabFold at the time) and folded them with full-length ASCL1.

Doing so informed us of some plausible regions on HUWE1 that may serve as the degron-

binding site, but more importantly, it nominated the C-terminus of ASCL1 as the putative degron

(Figure 2.6A). In addition to the conserved basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) domain of ASCL1,

we found that the second most conserved region was the C-terminus (Figure 2.6B), suggesting

its functional importance. We hypothesized that the C-terminal region of ASCL1 harbors its

primary degron. To confirm our hypothesis, we overexpressed WT ASCL1-GFP-IRES-mCherry

or C-terminus deleted ASCL1-GFP-IRES-mCherry into CORL47s, a human SCLC line, and

performed immunoprecipitation experiments coupled to a mass spectrometry-based readout. We

found that C-terminus deleted mutants completely lost their interaction with HUWE1 and the

26S proteasome (Figure 2.6C and Figure 2.6D). Conversely, we found increased interactions

with histones and DNA-binding proteins, indicating that mutants lacking the C-terminus may

accumulate on chromatin potentially due to reduced degradation (Figure 2.6C and Figure


<!-- Page 57 -->


38

CORL47 (human SCLCs) and 1014 (mouse SCLC) and showed that deletion of the C-terminus

significantly prolonged ASCL1’s half-life in stark contrast to the acute degradation of WT

ASCL1 upon CHX treatment (Figure 2.6E and Figure 2.6F). Furthermore, transplantation of

the C-terminus onto GFP was sufficient to induce degradation of GFP at the same rate as full-

To test whether the C-terminus is required for function, we asked whether reintroduction of WT

or C-terminal mutants could rescue the proliferation defects observed in ASCL1 KO lines. First,

we confirmed ASCL1 knockout and the successful overexpression with our reintroduced vectors

control guide (Figure 2.7B). Overexpression of WT ASCL1 rescued cell growth phenotypes

(Figure 2.7C) while C-terminus mutants could not (Figure 2.7D). These data imply that the C-

terminus is required for proper protein function, presumably through the successful execution of

Chapter 2.9: Systematic identification of activating mutations on HUWE1 that enhance

ASCL1 degradation using base-editing screens

There is strong genetic evidence that inducing the degradation of ASCL1 would lead to

therapeutic benefit for SCLC patients. However, we are limited in practice as TFs often do not

contain stereotypical drug-like pockets that are amenable to small molecule binding. Finding

functional regions on HUWE1 that lead to enhanced ASCL1 degradation could therefore be a

promising strategy as it may inform where exactly to place a molecule. To do so, we conducted a

saturating base-editing screen against HUWE1 in the same SCLC mouse 1014 ASCL1 reporter

line used in our initial CRISPR knockout screens. By sorting for the bottom 5% of ASCL1-

mCherry, BFP+ cells, we could enrich for mutations on HUWE1 that lead to enhanced

degradation of ASCL1 (Figure 2.8A). From this screen, we identified mutations on a

concentrated stretch of amino acids near the N-terminal region of HUWE1 (723-732). Given the

large size of HUWE1, it was shocking and gratifying to see this single region light up from our

screen. Next, we validated enhanced degradation of ASCL1 by introducing specific base-edit

mutations to cells and creating cell lines derived from single-cell clones followed by flow

cytometry analysis (Figure 2.8B). Through western blot analysis, we further validate three lines

showing decreased baseline levels of ASCL1 with an accelerated rate of degradation upon CHX

treatment compared to cells transduced with two different non-targeting control guides (Figure

2.8C). To generalize our findings to other HUWE1 substrates, we also saw reduced MYCL

(driver of some SCLCs) levels with reduced half-life in the mutants as well (Figure 2.8C). We

speculated that these mutations may lead to enhanced ubiquitination by HUWE1, leading to

increased substrate degradation. To test this hypothesis, we overexposed ASCL1-immunostained


<!-- Page 62 -->


43

blots to detect polyubiquitinated ASCL1 in WT or base-edited cells in the presence or absence of

MG-132, a proteasome inhibitor. We demonstrate that base-edited lines with these ‘activating’

HUWE1 mutations exhibited enhanced ubiquitination of ASCL1 upon proteasomal inhibition

(Figure 2.8D). These studies validate our hits from the base-editing screen and demonstrate that

these mutations lead to enhanced ubiquitination of ASCL1 by HUWE1 followed by its

subsequent degradation. These results motivated us to investigate the structural basis of

enhanced ASCL1 degradation by HUWE1.

Chapter 2.10 Identification of a previously unresolved regulatory helix on HUWE1 that

guards a known substrate binding pocket

Upon closer investigation, we noticed that all activating mutations were charge-flip mutations in

which negative residues were mutated to positively charged ones. Excitingly, this stretch of

amino acids accumulated on an alpha helix that was not resolved in a previously published cryo-

EM structure (PDB: 7JQ9), owing to the inherently disordered nature of this region as predicted

by Swiss-Model and AlphaFold3 (Figure 2.9A). Overlapping our AlphaFold 3 model with this

previously published cryo-EM structure, we found that the unresolved helix packed tightly

against a region on HUWE1 that resembles a donut and that has been shown to be the binding

site of DDIT4, a well-characterized substrate (Figure 2.9B). Looking at the surrounding amino

acids in this donut region, we noticed a few basic residues that were near acidic amino acids on

the helix. Excitingly, another structure of HUWE1 with phosphorylated DDIT4 (pS19, pT23,

pT25) showed that the phosphorylated residues make contacts with these same basic amino acids

in the donut region and that non-phosphorylated DDIT4 peptide could not interact with

recombinant HUWE1115. Taken together, it is tempting to speculate that this helix acts as a

molecular bouncer that permits substrate entry and binding. For that reason, I termed this helix as

the bouncer helix.

Sample preparation and TMT-labeling

Frozen cell pellets were lysed using 8 M urea and 200 mM EPPS at pH 8.5 with protease

inhibitors. Samples were then sonicated using a probe sonicator (twenty 0.5-s pulses at level 3).

The total amount of protein per sample was determined using a BCA assay. A total of 35 μg of

protein was aliquoted for each condition. Protein extracts were reduced using 5-Tris (2-

carboxyethyl) phosphine hydrochloride (TCEP) for 15 min at RT. Samples were then treated

with 10 mM iodoacetamide for 30 min in the dark at RT followed by precipitation using

chloroform/methanol as previously described117. After precipitation, samples were digested

overnight using LysC and trypsin (1:100 enzyme/protein ratio) at 37 °C using a ThermoMixer set

to 1,200 rpm. Following overnight digestion, peptides were labeled with TMTpro 18-plex

reagents at a 1:2 ratio by mass (peptides/TMT reagents) for 1 h with constant shaking at

1,200 rpm. Excess TMT reagent was quenched using hydroxylamine (0.3% final concentration)

for 15 min at RT. Next, samples were mixed 1:1 across all TMT channels and the pooled sample

was fully dried in a Speedvac.


<!-- Page 79 -->


60

Basic pH reversed-phase fractionation of TMT-labeled peptides

A 100-mg Sep-Pak solid-phase extraction cartridge was used to desalt the dried, pooled peptide

sample, as previously described117. The desalted peptide sample was dried in the Speedvac,

resuspended (10 mM ammonium bicarbonate, 5% acetonitrile, pH 8.0 buffer) and fractionated

into a 96-deep-well plate with basic pH reversed-phase HPLC using an Agilent 300 extend C18

column, and a 50 min linear gradient in 13–43% buffer (10 mM ammonium bicarbonate, 90%

acetonitrile, pH 8.0) at a flow rate of 0.250 ml min–1. The fractionated peptide mixture was

combined into 24 fractions as previously described and were desalted using StageTips117.

Samples were resuspended in 10 μl of 5% acetonitrile and 5% FA and were injected for analysis

on an Orbitrap Eclipse utilizing a high-resolution MS2-based method.

Liquid chromatography and tandem mass spectrometry

Mass spectrometry data were collected using a Orbitrap Eclipse mass spectrometer (Thermo

Fisher Scientific, San Jose, CA) coupled with Neo Vanquish liquid chromatograph. Peptides

were separated on a 100 μm inner diameter microcapillary column packed with ∼35cm of

Accucore C18 resin (2.6 μm, 150 Å, Thermo Fisher Scientific). For each analysis, we loaded ~2

μg onto the column. Peptides were separated using a 90 min gradient of 5 to 29% acetonitrile in

0.125% formic acid with a flow rate of 400 nL/min. The scan sequence began with an Orbitrap

MS1 spectrum with the following parameters: resolution 60K, scan range 350-1350, automatic

gain control (AGC) target 100%, maximum injection time “auto,” and centroid spectrum data


<!-- Page 80 -->


61

type. We use a cycle time of 1s for MS2 analysis which consisted of HCD high-energy collision

dissociation with the following parameters: resolution 50K, AGC 200%, maximum injection

time 86ms, isolation window 0.6 Th, normalized collision energy (NCE) 36%, and centroid

spectrum data type. Dynamic exclusion was set to automatic. The FAIMS compensation voltages

(CV) were -40, -60, and -80V.

For data searches the open-source Comet algorithm (release_2019010), following a previously

described pipeline, and a customized FASTA-formatted database incorporating common

contaminants and reversed sequences (Uniprot Human or Mouse, 2021), were used118–121. The

ensuing parameters were employed: 50 PPM precursor tolerance, fully tryptic peptides, fragment

peptide N-termini, carbamidomethylation of cysteine residues (+57.0214 Da) included as static

modification and oxidation of methionine residues (+15.9949 Da) included as a variable

modification. To achieve a false discovery rate (FDR) of <1%, the peptide spectral matches were

filtered using linear discriminant analysis with a target-decoy strategy. Further filtration ensured

a final protein-level FDR of 1% at the dataset level, and proteins were grouped. Reporter ion

intensities were adjusted to rectify impurities during the synthesis of different TMT reagents in

alignment with the specifications of the manufacturer. Each MS2 spectrum required a total sum

signal-to-noise (S/N) of all reporter ions of 180 for quantification. The S/N measurements of

peptides corresponding to proteins were summed and normalized to ensure equal loading across

all channels. Finally, protein abundance measurements were scaled to achieve a summed signal-

Chapter 2.15: Conclusion

We highlight in this chapter the power of combining mass spectrometry, TMT reagents, and

potent UPS inhibitors to systematically classify the short-lived proteome into distinct,

mechanistically defined degradation pathways. This work establishes a community-wide

resource that now enables the in-depth decoding of hundreds of newly categorized short-lived

proteins.

Using ASCL1 as an example, we present a generalizable framework illustrating how initial

insights from this degradation atlas can serve as a springboard to further the mechanistic

understanding of how a specific short-lived protein is degraded. Through an interdisciplinary

approach, we first identified the E3 ligase regulator of ASCL1 using a genome-wide CRISPR

screen in ASCL1 stability reporter lines. AlphaFold modeling then pinpointed the degron motif

recognized by HUWE1, and base-editing screens revealed the underlying logic of HUWE1

substrate recognition.

We discovered that a negatively charged regulatory helix, termed the bouncer helix, likely

guards this substrate-binding pocket, packing tightly against it under resting conditions. Base-

editing mutations that mutated these acidic residues within the bouncer helix to basic ones

enhanced ASCL1 degradation, consistent with a model in which the helix must move aside to

permit substrate binding. AlphaFold 3 modeling further supports this dynamic displacement

upon substrate co-folding, observed not only for ASCL1 but also for MYCL, DDIT4, SCNM1,

and C16orf72/HAPSTR1 (all known HUWE1 substrates).


<!-- Page 83 -->


64

We are now validating this mechanism biochemically and structurally to confirm our proposed

model of HUWE1–substrate interaction. Collectively, these findings suggest a unifying

mechanism for HUWE1 substrate recognition and offer a blueprint for pharmacologically

“activating” HUWE1 to enhance ASCL1 degradation potentially through small molecules that

displace the bouncer helix.

## Abstract

Live cell activity-based protein profiling (ABPP) with mass spectrometry enables the unbiased,

proteome-wide quantification of compound reactivity, yet resulting datasets often suffer from

low data completeness for high-priority targets and do not give users the option to measure

compound-induced protein changes within the same screening assay. To address these

limitations, we developed CysDig, an enrichment-free chemoproteomics platform for targeted

covalent drug discovery in live cells. Using the CysDig platform, we screened 288 cysteine-

reactive electrophiles against 300 functionally annotated cysteine sites. From this screen, we

identified covalent binders that liganded dozens of sites and identified multiple instances of acute


<!-- Page 86 -->


67

compound-induced protein degradation of ACAT1. We validated a molecule that engaged with

the active site of the HECT E3 ligase HUWE1 and showed that chemical inhibition stabilized

known substrates. Together, these findings establish CysDig as a powerful, targeted platform for

live cell covalent drug screening, expanding the current repertoire of available approaches for

ligand discovery in live cells.


<!-- Page 87 -->


68

## Introduction

Covalent molecules can irreversibly or reversibly modify proteins, providing chemical tools to

probe protein function and promising therapeutic modalities for human disease122. The increasing

number of covalent drug approvals continues to ignite the search for additional covalent

chemical starting points for previously considered “undruggable” targets123. The discovery of

these ligands is realized by a diverse repertoire of available methods124, with activity-based

protein profiling (ABPP) coupled to mass spectrometry providing an unbiased readout to

quantify covalent molecule binding on a proteome-wide scale108.

In a standard cysteine ABPP experiment, a covalent molecule competes with an enrichable

cysteine-reactive probe, and the resulting reduction in probe labeling relative to a control serves

as an indirect readout of compound engagement at that cysteine site. Throughput can be

significantly increased using tandem mass tag (TMT)-enabled multiplexing, which allows

simultaneous analysis of up to 18 samples in a single mass spectrometry run125. We and others

have leveraged this approach to profile proteome-wide cysteine reactivity of electrophilic

fragments in both live cells and lysates108–110,126–128.

Current cysteine profiling workflows enable broad, unbiased assessment of compound

engagement across the human proteome, offering unprecedented coverage of the cysteinome.

However, despite this depth, these workflows often suffer from high rates of missing values,

particularly for cysteine sites of functional or therapeutic interest. This limitation is especially

apparent in large-scale experiments, where high data completeness is critical for comparative

analysis or compound hit identification in the context of drug screens. Moreover, the requirement


<!-- Page 88 -->


69

for cysteine enrichment precludes the ability to simultaneously quantify protein abundance in the

same assay—an important consideration in live cell studies where compound treatment may

induce downstream proteomic changes that inform mechanism of action129.

To this end, we developed CysDig, an enrichment-free chemoproteomics platform that integrates

GoDig112, a TMT-based targeted proteomics strategy, within the context of cysteine-electrophile

treatment. The method relies on the observation that covalent modification of a cysteine by a

compound prevents alkylation by iodoacetamide (IAA) during standard proteomic sample

preparation. By directly targeting IAA-labeled cysteine-containing peptides, CysDig obviates the

need for enrichment and enables stoichiometric quantification of compound occupancy at

targeted cysteine sites130. Critically, omitting the enrichment step now enables protein abundance

measurements, which is already a core feature of the original GoDig platform and validated

across several organisms112,131.

Here, we leveraged CysDig to screen an electrophilic fragment library in live cells against 300

user-selected, functionally annotated cysteines belonging to proteins involved in various cellular

processes. We report that CysDig improved overall dataset completeness and identified covalent

fragments that engaged dozens of these targeted sites while clearly differentiating instances of

compound-induced acute protein depletion. To demonstrate the utility of our platform in

identifying functional covalent binders, we followed up with a fragment that engaged the

catalytic cysteine of the HECT E3 ligase HUWE1. Covalent docking and direct detection of the

covalent adduct confirmed active site engagement. Importantly, treatment with this compound

led to the dose-dependent accumulation of known HUWE1 substrates, providing evidence of


<!-- Page 89 -->


70

target inhibition. Collectively, these results establish CysDig as a modular, target-centric

chemoproteomics platform for covalent drug discovery in live cells.

## Results

Datasets from standard cysteine profiling workflows can have high missing values across

## experiments

Unbiased, proteome-wide cysteine profiling methods are stochastic in nature and often return

datasets with a high instance of missing values across experiments. For example, in three

previously conducted live cell TMT-ABPP campaigns, data completeness for cysteine-

containing peptides from proteins involved in key regulatory processes such as transcription

(Fig. 3.1a), phosphorylation (Fig. 3.1b), and proteostasis (Fig. 3.1c) ranged from 57-70%109.

High levels of missing values increase false negative rates, ultimately limiting the chances of

identifying chemical hits for downstream validation and development. We reasoned that

targeting a few hundred user-defined cysteine-containing peptides using a targeted proteomics

strategy would improve overall dataset data completeness.

To evaluate whether enrichment-free compound engagement data are comparable to those

obtained from conventional enrichment-based workflows, we performed a paired experiment

using both whole proteome (enrichment-free) and TMT-ABPP (enrichment-based) approaches

on the same K562 cell lysates treated with increasing doses of two previously characterized scout

quantified across the two datasets, we targeted 363 cysteine-containing peptides by using

represent the type of unfractionated, complex sample that we would generate for our CysDig

platform when conducting covalent drug screens (Fig S3.1b). Encouragingly, cysteine

The CysDig strategy for plate-based, enrichment-free targeted screens in live cells

The general workflow for CysDig is shown in Figure 3.2. We conducted a CysDig-enabled

screen in K562 cells. Cells were treated with cysteine-targeting electrophiles for 3 hr and then

prepared for CysDig analysis (Fig. 3.2a). Our library consisted of 288 compounds in total: 128

chloroacetamides-based and 160 acrylamides-based warhead-containing compounds

(Supplementary Table S2). The average molecular weight of the library was 231.2 Da (Fig.

S3.2). In comparison to enrichment-based and untargeted TMT-ABPP, there is no need to use

enrichment reagents such as DBIA, which streamlines sample preparation to only two days. For

this screen, we selected 300 peptides containing functionally annotated cysteines across proteins

involved in key cellular processes such as metabolism, intracellular signaling, protein quality

control, and genome regulation. We reasoned that compound binding at many of these given

cysteines would likely cause a functional and measurable change in protein activity. Thus, hits

from this screen, upon validation, could be used as chemical starting points for downstream

probe development.

Characterization of a HUWE1 active site inhibitor


<!-- Page 97 -->


78

Among the liganded cysteines identified in our screen were several cysteines known to play

regulatory or catalytic roles in protein function. Given the central role of the ubiquitin-

proteasome system (UPS) in maintaining protein homeostasis141 and its growing prominence as a

therapeutic target71, we focused on liganded cysteine sites within this pathway. Specifically, E3

ligases are attractive targets because modulating their activity can directly influence the stability

of their protein substrates such as tumor suppressors or oncogenes. Moreover, E3 ligases are

increasingly being co-opted as modular components in targeted protein degradation platforms

such as PROTACs, making covalent binders to these enzymes valuable both as functional probes

and as starting points for the design of heterobifunctional degraders80.

The human genome encodes 28 HECT E3 ligases, many of which regulate critical cellular

processes yet remain relatively underexplored from a chemical biology perspective. Unlike

RING-type E3s, HECT ligases directly form a covalent thioester intermediate with ubiquitin via

a conserved catalytic cysteine, rendering them mechanistically well-suited for covalent

inhibition142. While a handful of inhibitors have been reported for this class of proteins143–147, no

covalent active site binders have been characterized for any HECT E3 ligase. We prioritized the

HECT E3 ligase HUWE1 as this ligase regulates protein complex quality control, the DNA

damage response, cell proliferation, and apoptosis148. Notably, its dysregulation has been

implicated in both neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer149.

From our screen, we identified 33 chloroacetamide-containing electrophiles that bound the

HUWE1 active site with at least 50% occupancy. Among these, three exhibited strong


<!-- Page 98 -->


79

engagement, occupying greater than 75% of the active site (Fig. 3.5a). To prioritize selective

ligands for follow-up studies, we evaluated compound occupancy at two additional targeted

active-site cysteines from related HECT E3 ligases, UBE3A and UBE3C. Compound CL129

emerged as the most selective, showing strong engagement at HUWE1 with minimal off-target

binding to UBE3A or UBE3C (Fig. 3.5b, 3.5c). Additionally, unbiased, proteome-wide cysteine

profiling experiments in both HEK293T and K562 lysates treated with escalating doses of

CL129 demonstrate relatively few liganded sites (greater than 75% occupancy) (Fig. S3.3,

Supplementary Table S3). Moreover, we highlight dose-dependent engagement to the HUWE1

active site with relative selectivity over other quantified HECT E3 ligases (Fig. S3.4). We then

referred to a published crystal structure of the HUWE1 HECT domain150 for docking studies.

Covalent docking of CL129 to HUWE1’s catalytic Cys4341 predicted key non-covalent

interactions, including hydrogen bonding with Gly4316 and Glu4315, interaction with Arg4088,

and an anion–π stacking between the pyrimidine ring and Glu4315 (Fig. 3.5d). Mass

modification at the catalytic cysteine by CL129 (Fig. 3.5e). To evaluate the functional

consequences of HUWE1 active site inhibition, we conducted a six hr dose-dependent proteomic

Supplementary Table S4). Western blot analysis of DDIT4 further confirmed our proteomic

results (Fig. 3.5g). Together, these findings validate CL129 as a covalent binder of the HUWE1

active site.

Hybrid CysDig assays enable differentiation of cysteine engagement from acute protein

depletion events

In live-cell experiments, compound-induced changes in protein abundance can be misinterpreted

as target engagement, since dropout of cysteine-containing peptides occurs in both scenarios.

CysDig overcomes this limitation by simultaneously quantifying non-cysteine–containing

peptides for protein abundance measurements from the same sample. These hybrid CysDig

assays enable confident discrimination between compound binding and compound-induced

reductions in protein levels.

To illustrate the utility of a hybrid CysDig assay, we performed a second analysis of the same 36

TMT plexes that were analyzed previously. We retargeted a subset of functionally annotated

cysteine-containing peptides from our previous screen, along with corresponding non-cysteine-

containing peptides for robust protein abundance measurements (Fig. 3.6a). This strategy

enabled us to assess both compound occupancy at a specific cysteine site and the overall

abundance of that respective protein. As expected, for nearly all measured proteins, abundance

remained unchanged, confirming that most liganding events reflected true occupancy rather than

a change in protein levels (Fig. 3.6b, Supplementary Table S2). This result is unsurprising, as

the screen was conducted at a 3 hr timepoint, minimizing the likelihood of changes in protein

abundance. From this hybrid CysDig assay, we could confidently assign compound binding

without associated degradation to all molecules that liganded Cys283 of CKB (Fig. 3.6c).

chloroacetamide-containing PROTACs155. We confirmed this observation by treating cells with

cellular stress. Here, we show that hybrid CysDig assays can discriminate between cysteine

engagement and protein depletion events. Gaining such information-rich readouts at the

screening level supports efficient prioritization of chemical hits with the desired profile and

minimal off-target effects.

## Discussion

CysDig is an enrichment-free, targeted chemoproteomics platform in live cells. By applying a

TMT-based targeted data acquisition strategy (GoDig) within the context of cysteine-electrophile

treatment, CysDig overcomes key limitations of traditional cysteine profiling workflows—most

notably, high missing values and the inability to quantify compound-induced protein changes in

the same assay. Bypassing enrichment now simplifies sample preparation to two days, improves

data completeness, and allows users to build custom targeted proteomics assays for covalent drug

screens.

Using CysDig, we screened an electrophilic fragment library across 300 functionally annotated

cysteine sites in live cells. We demonstrate how our targeted data acquisition strategy returns

higher peptide-level data completeness compared to traditional TMT-ABPP workflows.

Importantly, we identify dozens of covalent binders as starting points for chemical probe

development upon further validation. We focused on HECT E3 ligases where cysteines play

essential catalytic roles in ubiquitin transfer142,156. Among three targeted HECT E3 ligases—

HUWE1, UBE3A, and UBE3C—we identified CL129 as a relatively selective covalent binder of

the HUWE1 active site located in the HECT domain that also upregulated the abundance of

known substrates in a dose-dependent manner. Despite high sequence conservation across HECT

domains, our findings suggests that there may be a unique opportunity to exploit subtle structural

differences for selective covalent engagement of HECT E3 ligases. Ultimately, these studies

validate the discovery capabilities of the CysDig platform, and moreover, nominate CL129 for

further development as a new covalent probe to further our understanding of HUWE1 biology

and explore the therapeutic potential of HUWE1 inhibition in various human disease models.


<!-- Page 104 -->


85

Looking forward, the CysDig platform is broadly extensible. With chemical libraries containing

the appropriate electrophilic warheads, this platform could be adapted to identify covalent

labeling of other nucleophilic residues—such as serine, tyrosine, lysine, or histidine—further

expanding the scope of covalent drug discovery beyond targeting cysteine157. Integration with

next-generation TMTpro-35plex reagents should also enhance throughput, enabling hundreds of

user-defined targets to be profiled in a single assay with fast and effective acquisition times of

under 3.5 min per sample158.

Standard live-cell ABPP workflows are constrained to short treatment times (< 3 hr) to minimize

confounding protein changes. With hybrid CysDig assays, screens could be extended to much

later timepoints while measuring both protein expression and cysteine engagement, opening new

opportunities to conduct biology-driven discovery campaigns in which the functional

consequences of binding can be measured such as substrate stabilization or pathway activation.

Because protein abundance is quantified in the same assay, CysDig allows confident

differentiation between true cysteine engagement and compound-induced protein abundance

changes. For example, ACAT1 was acutely degraded by more than 2-fold by thirteen distinct

chloroacetamides, suggesting its acute proteasome-dependent degradation may serve as a proxy

for electrophilic stress and should be included in covalent drug discovery campaigns to flag

electrophiles that may induce unwanted cellular stress. Notably, ACAT1 is not a short-lived

protein97, indicating that its rapid proteasome-mediated degradation by chloroacetamide-

containing electrophiles and the general alkylating agent iodoacetamide (IAA) is likely a

concerted mechanism that warrants further investigation. CysDig adds to the repertoire of

currently available platforms for small molecule covalent drug discovery. Its ability to


<!-- Page 105 -->


86

simultaneously measure cysteine occupancy and protein abundance within one unified assay now

empowers a new class of information-rich, biology-driven covalent drug screens at extended

timepoints.

## Methods

Cell culture

K562 cells were grown in RPMI-1640 medium supplemented with 10% FBS, 50 U/ml penicillin

and 50 U/ml streptomycin and incubated at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 incubator. Confluent dishes of

cells were either harvested and stored at -80 °C until required for lysis or they were plated into

96-well plates for downstream proteomics-based experiments.

Sample preparation for proteomic analyses

Paired in-lysate cysteine profiling and whole proteome comparison experiment

Frozen cell pellets were resuspended in lysis buffer (PBS, pH 7.4, 0.1% NP-40). A syringe

achieved by sonication with an EpiShear™ Probe Sonicator (Active Motif) for a total of 5 min (3

seconds on, 5 seconds off, at 50% amplitude) on ice. The crude lysate was centrifuged at 1400g

for 5 min at 4°C, after which the supernatant was collected into a separate tube. The protein


<!-- Page 106 -->

concentration was quantified using a BCA assay kit, and the lysate was subsequently diluted to a

concentration of 2 µg/µL with lysis buffer.

In each well of a 96-well plate, 25 µL of K562 lysate, with a total protein content of 50 µg, was

deposited. To this, 5 µL of a compound solution in lysis buffer was added to achieve a final

concentration ranging from 50 to 500 µM, followed by an incubation period of 1 hr. The probe-

treated lysate was subsequently divided into two equal portions.

For DBIA-based reactive cysteine profiling, 5 µL of a DBIA solution in lysis buffer was

introduced to reach a 500 µM concentration and incubated in darkness for 1 hr. For IAA-based

cysteine profiling, 5 µL of lysis buffer was added and incubated for 1 hr. Following this, 3 µL of

SP3 beads (a 1:1 mixture of hydrophobic and hydrophilic beads at 50 mg/mL) were

incorporated, along with 30 µL of ~98% ethanol supplemented with 20 mM DTT. The lysate-

bead mixture was subjected to a 10-minute incubation with gentle agitation before placing the

plate on a magnetic stand to remove the supernatant. A single wash with 80% ethanol was

performed, and the beads were re-suspended in 30 µL of lysis buffer supplemented with 20 mM

IAA. This preparation was then shaken vigorously in the dark for 30 min. Subsequently, 60 µL

of ~98% ethanol supplemented with 20 mM DTT was added to the mixture and the samples were

agitated gently before being washed twice with 80% ethanol. The aqueous phase was discarded,

and 30 µL of 200 mM EPPS buffer (pH 8.5) containing 0.25 µg of Lys-C was added. The

samples were left to incubate at room temperature for 3 hr. Finally, 5 µL of EPPS buffer with

0.25 µg of trypsin was incorporated, and the mixture was incubated with the beads at 37 °C

overnight.

Cells were processed in a plate-based format as previously described129. Briefly, compounds

were pre-dispensed into 96-well plates followed by the addition of 100,000 K562 cells (~10 𝜇g)

per well for 3 hr. Cells were spun down and washed twice with ice cold PBS. Cells were then

addition of 10mM iodoacetamide (IAA) in the dark for an additional 30 min. Lysates were

quenched with 20mM DTT and subjected to SP3 bead-based precipitation. Samples were then

TMT-labeled on bead and quenched with hydroxylamine followed by desalting via Sep-Pak prior
