spectrometry analysis117.

On-bead TMT-labeling of digested peptides

Digested peptides were labeled using TMTpro18-plex reagents as previously described125.

Briefly, peptides were labeled in a 1:2 ratio by mass (peptides/TMT reagents) for 1 hr with

shaking at 1,200 rpm. Excess TMT reagent was quenched with hydroxylamine (0.3% final

concentration) for 15 min at room temperature. Next, samples were mixed 1:1 across all TMT

channels and the pooled sample was dried using a Speedvac to ensure that all acetonitrile was

removed. The desalting of the resulting sample was performed using a 100 mg Sep-Pak column.

For whole proteome analyses, TMT-labeled peptides, approximately 100 µg, were fractionated

using an Agilent 300 Extend C18 column (3.5 μm particles, 2.1mm ID, and 250mm in length). A

50-minute linear gradient from 13 to 43% buffer B (90% acetonitrile, 10mM ammonium

Mass spectrometry-based data acquisition

LC-MS acquisition with real-time searching of the paired in-lysate cysteine profiling and whole

proteome experiments

Desalted samples were resuspended in LC-MS loading buffer (5% ACN and 5% FA) and loaded

on a 100-µm capillary column packed with 30 cm of Accucore 150 resin (2.6 μm, 150Å; Thermo

Fisher Scientific). Enriched cysteine samples were separated using a 180-min method on a

Proxeon NanoLC-1200 UPLC system. Data were collected using an RTS-MS3 method with a 3-

hr (DBIA-based cysteine profiling) or 2-hr (IAA-based whole proteome) gradient on an Orbitrap

Eclipse mass spectrometer coupled with a FAIMS Pro Duo interface. Data were collected

alternating between a set of three FAIMS compensation voltages (CVs). For the whole proteome

sample using IAA-only, only one set of CV values (-40, -60 and -80V) was used. For the

enriched cysteine sample, two sets of CV values (-60, -45 and -35V; -70, -55 and -30) were used.

MS1 scans were collected in the Orbitrap with a resolution setting of 60 K, a mass range of 400-

1600 m/z, a standard AGC, and a maximum injection time of 50 ms. RTS-MS3 scans were


<!-- Page 109 -->


90

acquired with a cycle time of 1 s. MS2 spectra were acquired by selecting the top ten most

abundant features via collision-induced dissociation in the ion trap using a standard AGC,

quadrupole isolation width of 0.5 m/z and a maximum ion accumulation time of 50 ms. Dynamic

exclusion was enabled with an exclusion duration of 120 s and a mass tolerance of ±7 p.p.m.

Resulting MS2 scans were searched in real time using the Comet search engine

(https://uwpr.github.io/Comet/) and the returned peptides were filtered using simple initial filters

that included: not matching a reversed-sequence, maximum PPM error <10, minimum cross

correlation of 0.5, minimum delta Corr of 0.10 and minimum peptide length of 7. If peptide

spectra matched those criteria above, an SPS–MS3 scan was inserted using up to 10 b- and y-

type fragment ions as precursors with a 500% AGC of 200 K for a maximum of 200ms, with a

normalized collision energy setting of 45.

LC-MS acquisition with real-time targeted chemoproteomics assays using GoDig

GoDig was run on the data collection computer connected to the instrument as previously

described112. Experiments used a 105-min gradient (120-min method). Note that the instrument

method only included Orbitrap MS1 scans (resolution of 120K; mass range 400−1500 m/z; AGC

target 2e5; max injection time of 50 ms; a single FAIMS CV of -60 V). All other scan types with

CV values at -40, -60 and -80, including prescans, ion trap MS2, Orbitrap MS2, and Orbitrap

MS3 scans were prompted for insertion via the API using the GoDig software. Peptide targets,

elution and spectral libraries were loaded into GoDig.

GoDig monitors each collected MS1 spectrum in real time with the possibility of inserting 5

different scan types for different uses112:


<!-- Page 110 -->


91

1) GoDig injects CV-specific prescans for each FAIMS CV value needed in addition to the

one being collected by the instrument method. These are used to set the AGC.

2) Every 15 s, GoDig selects and fragments the top 6 precursors in the most immediate MS1

scan to collect fast ion trap MS2 scans. The resulting scans are searched and mapped to

the elution library. Their elution bins are retrieved and used to calibrate the current

elution point.

3) In parallel, GoDig sends ion trap PRM scans for targets within the calibrated elution

window (±3 bin). Depending on the run length, bins represent between 15 to 30 s of

elution time. The returned PRMs are matched in real time to theoretical fragments of

specific targets (detection).

4) Upon matching a certain number of fragments in the ion trap PRM, GoDig prompts the

collection of Orbitrap MS2 scans with a maximum injection time of 900 ms to

accommodate weak signals. Fragment ions are matched and cosine-correlated to the

library spectrum for the target peptide (identification).

5) When cosine similarity is greater than 0.9 and more than 60% of the fragments with a

relative abundance greater than 50% in the library spectrum are present in the

experimental spectrum, GoDig selects SPS-ions that pass a fixed purity threshold and

inserts a custom SPS-MS3 scan (quantification). Maximum injection time is set to 2,000

ms in order to accommodate even very weak signals.

Chapter 4: Conclusions and future directions


<!-- Page 116 -->


97

Conclusions and future directions concerning the short-lived protein degradation atlas

Here, I have developed a multiplexed chemoproteomics assay to systematically reveal the

degradation pathways of the short-lived proteome in a given cell line. This approach gave us the

first glimpse of how the short-lived proteome is degraded and revealed many interesting insights

into the overall logic behind SLP degradation. We found that most proteins are degraded by the

proteasome largely in a ubiquitin-dependent manner. Almost all transcription factors are

degraded by the proteasome in a ubiquitin-dependent manner. Of note, we discover dozens of

new ubiquitin-independent proteasome substrates and found that they exhibit the fastest form of

degradation in the cell and are generally smaller than other SLPs. SLP degradation by the

lysosome appears to occur almost equally in a ubiquitin-dependent (mostly membrane signaling

proteins) and ubiquitin-independent manner (mostly membrane structural proteins). A subset of

the SLPome was found to be degraded by both pathways. These proteins are mostly found on the

ER and may reflect the unique biology that occurs at this organelle (ERphagy and ERAD).

In future iterations of this assay, additional chemical inhibitors can be incorporated to further

dissect the mechanisms governing short-lived protein (SLP) degradation. In unpublished work,

we have already employed p97, kinase, and sumoylation inhibitors to refine the classification of

degradation pathways within the short-lived proteome. Looking ahead, the advent of TMT 35-

plex reagents enables next-generation degradome profiling that can integrate an expanded panel

of perturbations in a single experiment. These reagents also allow systematic interrogation of

protein degradation dynamics as cells transition through distinct biological states such as viral

infection, differentiation, or apoptosis.


<!-- Page 117 -->


98

While the degradomics assay described here can delineate mechanistic degradation pathways at

scale, achieving finer resolution of substrate relationships within the proteostasis network

remains a key frontier. Fully decoding the degradome will require identifying the specific ligases

and regulatory proteins that govern the turnover of individual substrates. Integrating genetic

perturbations with high-throughput proteomic readouts offers a powerful approach to meet this

challenge enabling degradome mapping at unprecedented resolution and providing a detailed

blueprint of the cellular degradation machinery.

Conclusion concerning the regulation of ASCL1 by HUWE1

In close collaboration with the Oser Lab, we demonstrated the power of our degradome atlas as a

discovery platform that provides initial and often mechanistically revealing insights into how

specific proteins are degraded. From this resource, we found that ASCL1 is degraded by the

proteasome in a ubiquitin-dependent but CRL-independent manner. A genome-wide CRISPR

screen then identified HUWE1, a HECT-type E3 ligase, as the principal regulator of ASCL1

stability. We discovered that HUWE1 binds to the C-terminus of ASCL1 to mediate its

degradation. This sequence is both necessary for HUWE1 recognition and sufficient to confer

short half-life when fused to GFP.

Base-editing screens further illuminated functional hotspots within HUWE1 that modulate

substrate degradation. Strikingly, charge-flipping mutations within one distinct region of

HUWE1 enhanced ASCL1 degradation. AlphaFold modeling revealed that this region forms a

helix that likely guards a degron-binding pocket that has been preiously shown to be the binding


<!-- Page 118 -->


99

region of DDIT4, a well-characterized HUWE1 substrate. To test the generality of this

mechanism, we examined other known HUWE1 substrates and found that these same mutations

also promoted the degradation of MYCL, a transcription factor that we found to also be regulated

by HUWE1. Together, these findings identify a bona fide degron-binding site within HUWE1

whose accessibility is regulated by a negatively charged “bouncer helix,” providing a new

framework for understanding and potentially pharmacologically modulating HUWE1-substrate

interactions.

Structural studies are now underway to elucidate how ASCL1 engages the putative degron-

binding pocket of HUWE1 and how the bouncer helix dynamically repositions in response to

substrate binding. In parallel, we are exploring pharmacological strategies to displace the

bouncer helix as a means to enhance HUWE1-mediated degradation of ASCL1. This approach

could offer a novel therapeutic avenue for small-cell lung cancer (SCLC).

Conclusions concerning the CysDig platform

By applying a targeted proteomic workflow to covalent drug discovery, we have overcome one

of the major limitations of traditional unbiased acquisition methods—missing data. Notably, our

CysDig platform eliminates the need for cysteine enrichment, enabling dual measurement of

compound binding and corresponding changes in protein abundance within a single, unified

assay. This design makes CysDig particularly powerful for discovering compounds that

modulate the proteostasis network, as it directly quantifies the functional consequences of

covalent engagement on protein stability.


<!-- Page 119 -->


100

The utility of this platform will continue to expand as our understanding of proteostasis-mediated

degradation deepens. Advances such as library-free acquisition methods, higher-plex TMT

reagents, and improved mass spectrometry instrumentation will further enhance CysDig’s

throughput, sensitivity, and ease of use. Looking ahead, the same targeted framework could be

extended beyond cysteine chemistry to explore covalent ligands engaging other reactive amino

acids. Collectively, these innovations position CysDig as a next-generation discovery engine for

accessing previously “undruggable” targets.

Finally, structural studies of the covalent probe CL129 bound to the catalytic site of HUWE1 are

underway, with the goal of optimizing this molecule for potency and selectivity. These efforts

aim to establish CL129 as a first-in-class covalent probe for activity-based protein profiling

(ABPP) and as a potential therapeutic lead for HUWE1-dependent cancers.
